title: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 2
text:
How to use this book
If you have taken P-Chem 1 at Florida Tech, you should already be familiar with this format. Everything we did with the Live Textbook of P-Chem 1 will be happening this semester with P-Chem 2. Please read this book carefully, since everything that will be in your exams is explained here. Since this book is specifically tailored for the CHM 3002 course at Florida Tech, there are no superfluous parts. In other words, everything in it might be subject to question in the quizzes and the final exam.

Definitions and exercises are usually numbered and are highlighted in the text in this format (lighter grey, indented, and following a grey vertical bar). Please study the definitions carefully since they are fundamental concepts that will be used several times in the remainder of the text, and they will be subject to quizzes and exams. Exercises are essential for cementing the concepts, and you should attempt to execute them first without looking at the solution. Even if you were able to solve an exercise on your own, always read the solution after, since it might contain additional explanations expanding the main concepts in the text.

Navigating the book should be straightforward. On each page, there is a useful sidebar on the left that gives you an overview of all chapters, and a toolbar at the top with important tools. Arrows to shift between chapters might also be present, depending on your browser. If you are old-school and prefer a pdf, you can download a printout by clicking on the toolbar’s corresponding icon. If you are really old-school and prefer a printed book, the best solution is to download the pdf and print it yourself. It is a LaTeX book, and I can promise you it will look good on paper. However, I cannot provide physical copies to each student. In the toolbar, you will find a useful search box that is capable of searching the entire book. The most adventurous will find in the toolbar a link to the raw GitHub source code. Feel free to head on over there and fork the book.
The appendices at the end of the book review the mathematical tools that we use (Appendix A — Mathematical Toolkit), collect physical constants and unit conversions (Appendix B — Physical Constants and Unit Conversions), and suggest further reading for when you want a second explanation or more depth (Appendix C — Further Reading and References).
A note on the use of AI. The November 2026 revision of this book was prepared with the help of Claude Code (Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5), an AI assistant. The book, its structure, its scope, and its approach to teaching quantum chemistry are my own, developed over several years of teaching this course. In the revision, I used the AI as an assistant: to proofread the text, to rephrase passages, to draft new sections, figures, examples, and review questions following my outline and instructions, and to write the code for the computed and interactive figures. Every change was reviewed, corrected or rewritten, and approved by me, and I take full responsibility for the content of the book, including any remaining errors.

title: 1  Brief Summary of Classical Physics
text:
1.1 Classical Mechanics
Quantum mechanics cannot be derived from classical physics, but it was built by physicists who knew classical physics very well, and many of its ideas and equations are borrowed from it. Before discussing, in the next chapter, the experiments that classical physics could not explain, we will review the classical concepts that we will need the most: the description of motion through forces and through energy, the electrostatic interaction between charged particles, and the physics of waves.

1  Brief Summary of Classical Physics

title: 1  Brief Summary of Classical Physics
text:
1.1.1 Newtonian Formulation
Classical mechanics as formulated by Isaac Newton (1643–1727) is all about forces. Newtonian mechanics works well for problems where we know the forces and have a reasonable coordinate system. In these cases, the net force acting on a system at position \(\mathbf{r}\) in Cartesian 3-dimensional space \(\left\{ x,y,z \right\}\) is simply:
\[
F_{\mathrm{net}}(\mathbf{r}) = m\ddot{\mathbf{r}} = m \frac{d^2 \mathbf{r}}{dt^2}.
\tag{1.1}\]
Or, in other words, if we know the net force acting on a system of mass \(m\) at position \(\mathbf{r}\) at some time \(t_0\), we can use Eq. 1.1 to calculate the position of the system at any future (or past) time. We have completely determined the dynamical evolution of the system.1






Example 1.1: A ball tossed straight up (Newton)





A ball of mass \(m\) is at ground level and tossed straight up from an initial position \(x_0\) with an initial velocity \(\dot{x}_0\) and subject to gravity alone. Calculate the equation of motion for the ball (i.e. where is the ball going to be after some time \(t\)?).2
Solution: Since the only force acting on the ball is gravity, we can use the equation for the gravitational force to start our derivation:
\[
F_{\mathrm{gravity}}=-mg,
\tag{1.2}\]
with \(g\) the gravitational acceleration (\(g=9.8\; \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}\)). We can then replace this expression into Eq. 1.1, to obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
-mg &=m \ddot{\mathbf{r}} \\
-g &=\ddot{\mathbf{r}} \\
-g &=\frac{d\dot{\mathbf{r}}}{dt}. \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.3}\]
Working in a 1-dimensional case, we can replace \(\mathbf{r}\) with position \(x\) to obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
-mg &=m \ddot{x} \\
-g &=\ddot{x} \\
-g &=\frac{d\dot{x}}{dt}. \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.4}\]
which can then be integrated with respect to time, to obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
-g\int_{t=0}^{t} dt &=\int_{\dot{x}_0}^{\dot{x}} d\dot{x}\\
\dot{x} &= \dot{x}_0-gt\\
\frac{dx}{dt} &= \dot{x}_0-gt,\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.5}\]
which can be further integrated with respect to time, to give:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{x_0}^{x} dx &= \int_{t=0}^{t} \dot{x}_0 dt -g \int_{t=0}^{t}tdt\\
x &= x_0 + \dot{x}_0 t -\frac{1}{2}gt^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.6}\]
This final equation is the equation of motion for the ball, from which we can calculate the position of the ball at any time \(t\). Notice how the equation of motion does not depend on the mass of the ball!
Numerical problem: How much time will a ball ejected from a height of \(1 \;\mathrm{m}\) at an initial velocity of \(10 \;\mathrm{m/s}\) take to hit the floor?
We can use the equation of motion obtained above to solve this problem, and obtain for this specific case \(t\simeq2.14\;\mathrm{s}\).3



Newton’s equation is not the only way of writing the laws of classical mechanics. Physicists have developed other, equivalent formulations, which give exactly the same results but are more convenient for some problems. The most famous are the Lagrangian formulation, based on the difference between the kinetic and the potential energy of a system, and the Hamiltonian formulation, based on their sum.4 Only the second one will be important for us, because it is the one that quantum mechanics is built upon.


1.1.2 Hamiltonian Formulation
Newton’s mechanics is built around forces. Hamiltonian mechanics, instead, is built around energy. Its goal is to describe the motion of a system starting from a single function, the total energy, written in terms of where the particle is and how much momentum it has. This is exactly the starting point that we will use in quantum mechanics, which is why we need to get familiar with it now.
The first ingredient is the momentum of a particle of mass \(m\) moving with velocity \(\dot{x}\) (we will work in one dimension to keep things simple):
\[
p = m\dot{x}.
\tag{1.7}\]
Momentum carries the same information as velocity, but, as we will see in the next chapter, it is the quantity that appears naturally when we describe particles in quantum mechanics.
The second ingredient is the total energy of the system, which is the sum of the kinetic energy, \(K\), and the potential energy, \(V\):
\[
H = K + V.
\tag{1.8}\]
When we write this total energy as a function of the position, \(x\), and the momentum, \(p\), we call it the Hamiltonian of the system, and we use the symbol \(H\). Since the kinetic energy is \(K=\frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2\), and \(\dot{x}=p/m\), we can write \(K=\frac{p^2}{2m}\), and the Hamiltonian of a particle becomes:
\[
H(x,p) = \frac{p^2}{2m} + V(x).
\tag{1.9}\]
This equation is the most important result of this section. The first term depends only on the momentum, and it is the same for every system. The second term depends only on the position, and it is what makes each system different: a ball in the gravitational field of the Earth, an electron attracted by a nucleus, or two atoms connected by a chemical bond differ only in their potential energy, \(V(x)\).
Once we know the Hamiltonian, the motion of the system can be obtained from two simple equations, called Hamilton’s equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot{x}=\frac{dx}{dt} &= +\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, \\
\dot{p}=\frac{dp}{dt} &= -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.10}\]
These two equations are less mysterious than they look. If we apply them to Eq. 1.9, the first one gives \(\dot{x}=\frac{p}{m}\), which is just the definition of momentum, Eq. 1.7, read backwards. The second one gives \(\dot{p}=-\frac{dV}{dx}\). Since \(\dot{p}=m\ddot{x}\), and since minus the derivative of the potential energy is the force, \(F=-\frac{dV}{dx}\), this is just Newton’s equation, \(F=m\ddot{x}\), written in a different form. Hamilton’s equations, in other words, contain no new physics: they are a different way of organizing the same information, starting from the energy instead of the forces.






Example 1.2: The same ball, using the Hamiltonian





Let’s apply the Hamiltonian formulation to the same problem as in the previous example: a ball of mass \(m\) tossed straight up and subject only to gravity.
The potential energy of the ball at height \(x\) is \(V(x)=mgx\), so the Hamiltonian, Eq. 1.9, is:
\[
H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+mgx.
\tag{1.11}\]
Hamilton’s equations, Eq. 1.10, give:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot{x} &= \frac{\partial H}{\partial p} = \frac{p}{m}, \\
\dot{p} &=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial x} = -mg.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.12}\]
The second equation tells us that the momentum of the ball decreases at a constant rate, \(p(t)=p_0-mgt\), where \(p_0=m\dot{x}_0\) is the initial momentum. Replacing it in the first equation, we obtain \(\dot{x}=\dot{x}_0-gt\), and integrating once more we obtain the same equation of motion that we found with Newton’s method:
\[
x = x_0 + \dot{x}_0 t -\frac{1}{2}gt^2.
\tag{1.13}\]



So, if the Hamiltonian gives the same answers as Newton’s equation, why do we bother? There are two reasons, both important for what follows:

The Hamiltonian is the total energy, and the total energy is conserved. We can check this for the ball in the previous example: replacing \(p(t)\) and \(x(t)\) in Eq. 1.11, all the terms that depend on time cancel out, and \(H=\frac{p_0^2}{2m}+mgx_0\) at all times. As the ball rises, kinetic energy is converted into potential energy and vice versa, but their sum, \(H\), never changes. Energy, and not force, is the central quantity in chemistry, and the energy levels of atoms and molecules are what we measure in experiments.
The Hamiltonian is the bridge to quantum mechanics. In quantum mechanics we will not be able to talk about the trajectory of a particle, so Newton’s equation will be of little use. The Hamiltonian, on the other hand, will survive almost unchanged. In Chapter 6, we will see that the central equation of quantum mechanics, the Schrödinger equation, is obtained by taking Eq. 1.9 and replacing the momentum, \(p\), with a mathematical operation (a derivative) acting on a wave function.

title: 1  Brief Summary of Classical Physics
text:
1.2 Coulomb’s Law
Chemistry is, in the end, all about charged particles: positive nuclei and negative electrons. The force between them is described by Coulomb’s law, discovered by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785. For two point charges \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) at a distance \(r\) from each other, the force is:
\[
F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{r^{2}},
\tag{1.14}\]
where \(\varepsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\;\mathrm{C^2\,J^{-1}\,m^{-1}}\) is the vacuum permittivity, a constant that sets the strength of electric forces. The force acts along the line that joins the two charges, and Eq. 1.14 tells us two things:

The sign. If the two charges have the same sign, \(q_1q_2>0\) and the force is positive: the charges repel each other. If they have opposite signs, as for an electron and a nucleus, \(q_1q_2<0\) and the force is negative: the charges attract each other.
The distance dependence. The force decreases with the square of the distance: doubling the distance between the charges makes the force four times weaker.

You may also find the same law written in terms of the electric field, \(\mathbf{E}\). We can think of each charge as creating a field around itself, and of the other charge as feeling a force \(\mathbf{F}=q\,\mathbf{E}\) from that field. The two descriptions are equivalent, and we will mention the electric field again only when we discuss how light interacts with molecules (Chapter 13).

1.2.1 Electrostatic potential energy
In quantum mechanics, as we will see in Chapter 3, we do not work with forces, but with energies. So what we really need is the potential energy of two charges, \(V(r)\). This is the energy stored in the pair of charges, and it is equal to the work that we have to do to bring them from very far apart (where they do not interact, and \(V=0\)) to the distance \(r\). Since the force changes with the distance, this work is an integral:
\[
V(r) = -\int_{\infty}^{r} F(r')\,dr' = -\frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\infty}^{r}\frac{dr'}{r'^2} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{r}.
\tag{1.15}\]
(The minus sign is there because we push against the force: for two charges that repel, we need to do work to bring them closer, and the potential energy is positive.)
Eq. 1.15 is the most important result of this section, and it will appear in almost every chapter of this book. Notice how similar it is to Eq. 1.14, but with \(r\) instead of \(r^2\) in the denominator. As a consequence, the potential energy decreases with distance more slowly than the force does.
For an electron (\(q_1=-e\)) and a proton (\(q_2=+e\)), with \(e=1.602\times10^{-19}\;\mathrm{C}\), the potential energy is always negative, and it becomes more and more negative as the two particles get closer:
\[
V(r) = -\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,r}.
\tag{1.16}\]
To get a feeling for the numbers, at a distance of \(0.529\;\text{Å}\) (the typical size of a hydrogen atom, as we will see in Chapter 2), Eq. 1.16 gives \(V=-4.36\times10^{-18}\;\mathrm{J}\) per electron–proton pair, or \(-2625\;\text{kJ/mol}\). This is several times larger than the energy of a typical chemical bond (a few hundred kJ/mol), which tells us that the Coulomb interaction is more than strong enough to hold atoms and molecules together.

title: 1  Brief Summary of Classical Physics
text:
1.3 Classical Waves
The last ingredient of classical physics that we need is the description of waves. Waves are everywhere: on the surface of water, in a vibrating guitar string, in sound, and in light. As we will see in the next two chapters, the central idea of quantum mechanics is that particles such as electrons also behave like waves, and the mathematics of quantum mechanics is, to a large extent, the mathematics of waves.

1.3.1 Describing a wave
A wave is a disturbance that repeats itself in space and time. Think of a long rope that you shake up and down at one end: a pattern of crests and troughs travels along the rope, even though each piece of rope only moves up and down. A snapshot of such a wave is shown in Fig. 1.1. We can describe it with a few quantities:

The amplitude, \(A\), is the maximum displacement from the rest position.
The wavelength, \(\lambda\), is the distance between two neighboring crests (or troughs).
The frequency, \(\nu\), is the number of crests that pass by a fixed point every second. Its inverse, \(1/\nu\), is the period, the time between two crests.
The speed, \(v\), is how fast the crests move. Since one wavelength passes by every period, the three quantities are related by:

\[
v = \lambda\nu.
\tag{1.17}\]






Figure 1.1: A traveling wave at \(t=0\) (solid line) and a short time later (dashed line), showing its wavelength and amplitude. The pattern moves to the right with speed \(v\).



Mathematically, the displacement \(y\) of the rope at position \(x\) and time \(t\) for a wave moving to the right can be written as:
\[
y(x,t) = A\sin(kx-\omega t),
\tag{1.18}\]
where we have introduced two quantities that make the formulas simpler: the wave vector, \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\), which tells us how many radians the wave advances per unit length, and the angular frequency, \(\omega=2\pi\nu\), which tells us how many radians it advances per unit time. You can check that Eq. 1.18 repeats itself every time \(x\) increases by \(\lambda\) (at fixed \(t\)) or \(t\) increases by \(1/\nu\) (at fixed \(x\)), and that the crests move with speed \(v=\omega/k=\lambda\nu\).

A useful mathematical tool: complex waves
In quantum mechanics, waves are usually written using complex numbers instead of sines and cosines. The reason is Euler’s formula, which connects the exponential function with the trigonometric functions:
\[
e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta + i\sin\theta,
\tag{1.19}\]
where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\) is the imaginary unit (complex numbers are reviewed in Sec. A.1). Using this formula, we can write a wave as:
\[
y(x,t) = A\,e^{i(kx-\omega t)} = A\cos(kx-\omega t) + iA\sin(kx-\omega t),
\tag{1.20}\]
which contains both a cosine wave (the real part) and a sine wave (the imaginary part). The advantage is that exponentials are much easier to differentiate than sines and cosines: taking a derivative with respect to \(x\) simply multiplies the function by \(ik\), since \(\frac{d}{dx}e^{ikx}=ike^{ikx}\). We will start from exactly this form of a wave when we introduce the Schrödinger equation in Chapter 3.



1.3.2 The wave equation
Just as Newton’s equation describes the motion of a particle, there is an equation that describes the motion of a wave. For a wave moving along a string, it is called the classical wave equation:
\[
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2} = \frac{1}{v^2}\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}.
\tag{1.21}\]
The left-hand side measures how curved the string is at a given point, and the right-hand side measures how fast that point accelerates up or down. In words, the equation says that the more a piece of string is curved, the faster it accelerates back towards a straight line. We can check that Eq. 1.18 is a solution: taking two derivatives with respect to \(x\) gives \(-k^2y\), and taking two derivatives with respect to \(t\) gives \(-\omega^2y\). Replacing them in Eq. 1.21, we obtain \(-k^2y=-\frac{\omega^2}{v^2}y\), which is true as long as \(v=\omega/k\), the relation between speed, frequency, and wavelength that we already found.
An important property of the wave equation is that it is linear: if \(y_1(x,t)\) and \(y_2(x,t)\) are two solutions, their sum, \(y_1+y_2\), is also a solution. This is called the principle of superposition, and it means that when two waves meet, their displacements simply add up. If the crests of the two waves coincide (they are in phase), they reinforce each other and produce a larger wave, which is called constructive interference. If the crests of one wave coincide with the troughs of the other (they are out of phase), they cancel each other, which is called destructive interference. The two cases are shown in Fig. 1.2. Interference is the signature of wave behavior, and we will see in Chapter 8 that it is also observed for electrons.






Figure 1.2: Superposition of two waves with the same wavelength. Left: when the waves are in phase, they add up to a wave with twice the amplitude (constructive interference). Right: when they are out of phase, they cancel each other (destructive interference).





1.3.3 Standing waves on a string
Something very interesting happens when a wave is confined, as on a guitar string of length \(L\) fixed at both ends. The waves travel along the string, bounce back at the ends, and interfere with themselves. Most of them cancel out, and only a few special patterns survive. These patterns do not travel along the string; they just oscillate up and down in place, and they are called standing waves.
To find them, we look for solutions of the wave equation in which the shape of the string does not change, but only its size, which oscillates in time:
\[
y(x,t) = \psi(x)\cos(\omega t).
\tag{1.22}\]
Here \(\psi(x)\) describes the shape of the string, and \(\cos(\omega t)\) describes how it oscillates. Replacing Eq. 1.22 in the wave equation, Eq. 1.21, the time-dependent factor cancels out, and we are left with an equation for the shape only:
\[
\frac{d^2 \psi}{d x^2} = -k^2\psi(x), \qquad k=\frac{\omega}{v}.
\tag{1.23}\]
The solutions of this equation are sines and cosines, \(\psi(x)=a\sin(kx)+b\cos(kx)\). Now we use the fact that the string is fixed at both ends, which gives two boundary conditions:

At \(x=0\), the string cannot move, so \(\psi(0)=0\). Since \(\sin(0)=0\) and \(\cos(0)=1\), this requires \(b=0\), and \(\psi(x)=a\sin(kx)\).
At \(x=L\), the string cannot move either, so \(\psi(L)=a\sin(kL)=0\). If \(a=0\) the string does not vibrate at all, so we need \(\sin(kL)=0\), which is only true when \(kL\) is a whole multiple of \(\pi\).

The second condition can only be satisfied by special values of \(k\), and therefore of the wavelength, \(\lambda=2\pi/k\), and of the frequency, \(\nu=v/\lambda\):
\[
k_n = \frac{n\pi}{L}, \qquad \lambda_n = \frac{2L}{n}, \qquad \nu_n = \frac{nv}{2L}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
\tag{1.24}\]
and the corresponding shapes are:
\[
\psi_n(x) = a\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right).
\tag{1.25}\]
The first four standing waves are shown in Fig. 1.3.






Figure 1.3: The first four standing waves on a string of length \(L\) fixed at both ends (black squares). The solid and dashed lines show the string at its two extreme positions, and the light lines show intermediate positions. The nodes are reported as purple dots.



Three things in these results are worth noticing:

Quantization: a confined wave can only have certain wavelengths and frequencies, labeled by a whole number, \(n\). This is why a guitar string plays a definite note (the frequency with \(n=1\), called the fundamental) together with its overtones (\(n=2,3,\ldots\)), and not any frequency at all. Notice that nothing in the wave equation itself is quantized: the quantization comes entirely from the boundary conditions, i.e., from confining the wave.
Nodes: the standing wave with quantum number \(n\) has \(n-1\) points between the two ends where the string never moves, called nodes. The higher the frequency, the more nodes the wave has.
The link with quantum mechanics: in Chapter 4, we will solve the Schrödinger equation for an electron confined in a one-dimensional box, and we will obtain exactly the same functions as in Eq. 1.25, with the same conditions on the wavelength. The quantization of the energy of atoms and molecules has the same origin as the quantization of the notes of a guitar: a wave that is confined in a region of space.



1.3.4 Light as an electromagnetic wave
One more type of wave will be important for us: light. In the 19th century, James Clerk Maxwell showed that light is a wave of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, called an electromagnetic wave. In a vacuum, all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed, the speed of light, \(c=2.998\times10^8\;\text{m/s}\), so Eq. 1.17 becomes:
\[
c = \lambda\nu.
\tag{1.26}\]
Different wavelengths correspond to different types of radiation, which together form the electromagnetic spectrum: from radio waves (wavelengths of meters or more), to microwaves (millimeters to centimeters), infrared (micrometers), visible light (\(400\)–\(700\;\text{nm}\)), ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays (shorter than a billionth of a meter). In classical physics, the energy carried by an electromagnetic wave depends on its amplitude (the brighter the light, the more energy it carries), and not on its frequency. As we will see in the next chapter, this classical picture of light is one of the first things that quantum mechanics had to change.

title: 1  Brief Summary of Classical Physics
text:
1.4 Chapter Review

1.4.1 Key Ideas

Newton’s equation, \(F=m\ddot{x}\), determines the trajectory of a particle once we know the forces and the initial conditions.
The Hamiltonian, \(H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+V(x)\), describes the same physics through the total energy, which is conserved. It is the bridge to quantum mechanics.
Charged particles interact through the Coulomb potential energy, \(V(r)=\frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\), which is negative (attractive) for an electron and a nucleus.
Waves are described by their wavelength, frequency, and speed, \(v=\lambda\nu\), and they are conveniently written as complex exponentials using Euler’s formula.
A wave confined between two fixed points can only have certain wavelengths: confinement leads to quantization, and higher frequencies mean more nodes.



1.4.2 Study Questions
1. If we know the net force acting on a particle, and its position and velocity at one instant, Newton’s equation allows us to:

calculate only its average position
calculate only the probability of finding it at each position
calculate its position at any future (or past) time
calculate its energy, but not its position
calculate its position only if no force acts on it


2. The momentum of a particle of mass \(m\) moving with velocity \(\dot{x}\) is:

\(p=\frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2\)
\(p=m\ddot{x}\)
\(p=\dot{x}/m\)
\(p=mgx\)
\(p=m\dot{x}\)


3. Which of the following is the Hamiltonian of a particle of mass \(m\) moving in one dimension with potential energy \(V(x)\)?

\(H=\frac{p^2}{2m}-V(x)\)
\(H=m\ddot{x}\)
\(H=\frac{1}{2}mp^2+V(x)\)
\(H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+V(x)\)
\(H=p\,V(x)\)


4. Why is the Hamiltonian, rather than Newton’s equation, the starting point of quantum mechanics?

because it is easier to integrate than Newton’s equation
because it describes the system through its energy, which keeps its meaning even when trajectories do not
because it does not depend on the potential energy
because it gives different results from Newton’s equation for heavy particles
because forces do not exist in quantum mechanics


5. The Coulomb force between an electron and a proton is:

repulsive, because the two charges have opposite signs
zero, because the two charges cancel each other
attractive, because the two charges have opposite signs
attractive only at large distances
independent of the distance between the particles


6. The electrostatic potential energy \(V\) of two point charges \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) separated by a distance \(r\) is:

\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\)
\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} q_1 q_2 r\)
\(V = q_1 q_2 r^2\)
\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r}\)
\(V = \dfrac{q_1 + q_2}{r}\)


7. The speed \(v\), wavelength \(\lambda\), and frequency \(\nu\) of a wave are related by:

\(v=\lambda/\nu\)
\(v=\nu/\lambda\)
\(v=2\pi\lambda\nu\)
\(v=\lambda^2\nu\)
\(v=\lambda\nu\)


8. Euler’s formula, which allows us to write waves using complex exponentials, is:

\(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\)
\(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta\)
\(e^{i\theta}=\sin\theta+i\cos\theta\)
\(e^{\theta}=\cos\theta+\sin\theta\)
\(e^{i\theta}=i\cos\theta\sin\theta\)


9. A guitar string of length \(L\) is fixed at both ends. Which wavelengths can its standing waves have?

any wavelength
only \(\lambda_n=2L/n\), with \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\)
only \(\lambda=L\)
only wavelengths longer than \(2L\)
only \(\lambda_n=nL\), with \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\)


10. How many nodes (points that never move, not counting the two fixed ends) does the standing wave with quantum number \(n\) have?

\(n-1\)
\(n\)
\(n+1\)
\(2n\)
none

1.c, 2.e, 3.d, 4.b, 5.c, 6.d, 7.e, 8.a, 9.b, 10.a

1  Brief Summary of Classical Physics

title: 2  The Failure of Classical Physics
text:
2.1 Historical Context
In the previous chapter, we reviewed the fundamental concepts of classical physics. In this chapter, we will see how these concepts fail when applied to atoms and light, and how these failures led to the development of quantum mechanics.
By the end of the 19th century, many physicists believed that their job was almost done. Newton’s mechanics described the motion of everything from falling apples to planets, and Maxwell’s equations described light as an electromagnetic wave. Only a few small puzzles were left to solve. Within thirty years, those few small puzzles had brought down the whole classical picture of the microscopic world, and replaced it with quantum mechanics: the theory that is at the foundation of all of modern chemistry.
The first cracks came from the discovery that atoms are not indivisible. J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897, a year after Henri Becquerel had discovered radioactivity, which Marie and Pierre Curie then studied in depth. Atoms were clearly made of smaller charged pieces, and physicists started to build models of how these pieces fit together. Every attempt to describe them with classical physics, however, ran into contradictions. In 1911, Ernest Rutherford showed that the positive charge of an atom is concentrated in a tiny nucleus, with the electrons around it. According to classical electromagnetism, an electron orbiting a nucleus should continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus in a fraction of a second. Atoms, in other words, should not exist.
The key idea that resolved these contradictions was quantization. In 1900, Max Planck showed that he could explain the light emitted by hot objects if he assumed that energy is exchanged only in discrete amounts, or “quanta.” In 1905, Albert Einstein used the same idea to explain the photoelectric effect, proposing that light itself is made of quanta, later called photons. In 1913, Niels Bohr applied quantization to the hydrogen atom, assuming that the electron could move only on certain orbits with fixed energies, and that light is emitted or absorbed when the electron jumps between them. Bohr’s model reproduced the spectrum of hydrogen with remarkable accuracy, but it worked only for atoms and ions with a single electron, and it had no justification other than the fact that it worked. In 1924, Louis de Broglie suggested that, if light waves can behave like particles, then particles such as electrons might behave like waves.
A complete theory finally arrived in 1925–1926, in two different forms. Werner Heisenberg, together with Max Born and Pascual Jordan, developed matrix mechanics, a formulation based on arrays of numbers (matrices) that deals only with observable quantities, such as the frequencies and intensities of spectral lines. Shortly after, Erwin Schrödinger developed wave mechanics, based on the equation that now bears his name and that describes particles using waves. The two formulations looked completely different, but they were soon shown to be mathematically equivalent. Together, they form the theory that we will study in this textbook.
In the rest of this chapter, we will look in more detail at the experiments that classical physics could not explain, and at how their explanations led to the main ideas of quantum mechanics. These are the “ultraviolet catastrophe,” the photoelectric effect, the line spectra of atoms, and the wave-particle duality.

title: 2  The Failure of Classical Physics
text:
2.2 The Ultraviolet Catastrophe
Every object emits electromagnetic radiation, and the hotter the object, the more radiation it emits and the shorter its wavelengths. This is why a piece of metal heated in a flame first glows red, then orange, and then white. To study this radiation without having to worry about the details of a specific material, physicists use an idealized object called a black body, which absorbs all the radiation that hits it and emits radiation that depends only on its temperature. The radiation emitted by a black body at a few temperatures is shown in Fig. 2.1.






Figure 2.1: Intensity of the radiation emitted by a black body at three temperatures, calculated with Planck’s law (solid lines). The purple dots mark the maximum of each curve. The dashed line is the classical Rayleigh–Jeans prediction at 5800 K, which diverges at short wavelengths. The shaded region is the visible part of the spectrum.



Using classical electromagnetism and classical statistical mechanics, Lord Rayleigh and James Jeans derived an equation for the intensity of the radiation emitted by a black body at temperature \(T\) as a function of the wavelength \(\lambda\). The result, known as the Rayleigh–Jeans law, is:
\[
I(\lambda,T)={\frac {2ck_{\mathrm{B}}T}{\lambda^{4}}},
\tag{2.1}\]
where \(I\) is the intensity of the radiation (more precisely, the power emitted per unit area of the emitting surface, per unit solid angle, and per unit wavelength, a quantity called spectral radiance), \(c\) is the speed of light, \(k_{\mathrm{B}}\) is the Boltzmann constant, and \(T\) is the temperature in kelvins. This formula works well at long wavelengths, but it fails dramatically at short ones (dashed line in Fig. 2.1). If we take the limit for \(\lambda \rightarrow 0\) in Eq. 2.1, we obtain \(I \rightarrow \infty\). In other words, the shorter the wavelength (towards the UV and beyond), the more radiation the black body should emit, and the total energy emitted over all wavelengths should be infinite. This prediction is clearly absurd: if it were true, every warm object would be emitting an infinite amount of energy as UV light, X-rays, and gamma rays. This failure of classical physics is called the ultraviolet catastrophe (or Rayleigh–Jeans catastrophe).
Max Planck solved the problem in 1900 by making an assumption that had no justification in classical physics: the energy of the oscillating electrons that emit the radiation cannot take any value, but only integer multiples of a minimum amount proportional to the frequency \(\nu\) of the radiation:
\[
E = n h \nu = n h \frac{c}{\lambda},
\tag{2.2}\]
with \(n\) a positive integer. With this assumption, Planck obtained the following formula for the intensity:
\[
I(\lambda ,T)={\frac {2hc^{2}}{\lambda ^{5}}}{\frac {1}{e^{hc/(\lambda k_{\mathrm {B} }T)}-1}}.
\tag{2.3}\]
At short wavelengths, the exponential in the denominator grows much faster than \(\lambda^5\) decreases, and \(I\) goes to zero as \(\lambda \rightarrow 0\), in agreement with the experiments. (At long wavelengths, instead, \(e^{x}-1\approx x\), and Planck’s law reduces to the Rayleigh–Jeans law.) Physically, quantization works because at short wavelengths the minimum quantum of energy, \(hc/\lambda\), becomes much larger than the typical thermal energy, \(k_{\mathrm{B}}T\), and the high-frequency oscillations are simply too “expensive” to be excited. By fitting Eq. 2.3 to the experimental data, Planck also obtained the value of the new constant, \(h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \; \text{J s}\), which is now called the Planck constant.
Let’s look at what Fig. 2.1 tells us:

Color and temperature: as the temperature increases, the maximum of the curve moves to shorter wavelengths. The position of the maximum follows a simple rule, called Wien’s displacement law, which can be derived from Eq. 2.3: \(\lambda_\text{max}T = 2.898\times10^{-3}\;\text{m K}\). The surface of the Sun (\(T\approx5800\;\text{K}\)) has its maximum at \(\lambda_\text{max}\approx500\;\text{nm}\), in the middle of the visible region (our eyes evolved to see the light that the Sun emits the most). An incandescent light bulb (\(T\approx3000\;\text{K}\)) has its maximum at about \(970\;\text{nm}\), in the infrared, which is why it looks yellowish and why most of its energy is wasted as heat. Our bodies (\(T\approx310\;\text{K}\)) emit mostly at about \(9{,}000\;\text{nm}\), in the infrared, where thermal cameras can see it.
Brightness and temperature: the area under each curve, which is the total power emitted, grows very quickly with temperature (as \(T^4\), a result known as the Stefan–Boltzmann law). Doubling the temperature of an object makes it emit sixteen times more energy.
Where classical physics fails: the classical and quantum curves agree at long wavelengths, where the quanta \(h\nu\) are small compared to \(k_\mathrm{B}T\) and the energy behaves as if it were continuous. They disagree completely at short wavelengths, where the quanta are large. This is a pattern that we will see again: quantum effects become important when the spacing between energy levels is large compared to the thermal energy.

Planck himself considered quantization a mathematical trick rather than a property of nature, and the idea was not taken seriously until Einstein used it to explain the photoelectric effect.

title: 2  The Failure of Classical Physics
text:
2.3 The Photoelectric Effect
When light shines on a clean metal surface, electrons can be ejected from it. This phenomenon is called the photoelectric effect. It was first observed by Heinrich Hertz in 1887, and studied in detail by Philipp Lenard around 1900. Albert Einstein explained it in 1905, proposing that light energy is quantized into discrete particles, called photons, each with an energy proportional to its frequency.
To see why an explanation was needed, let’s start from the classical prediction. As we saw at the end of Chapter 1, in classical physics light is a continuous electromagnetic wave, and the energy that it delivers every second depends on its amplitude (its brightness, or intensity), and not on its frequency. If we apply this picture to the photoelectric effect, we expect the electrons in the metal to absorb energy from the wave continuously, and to be ejected when they have accumulated enough of it to escape the surface. A brighter light delivers energy faster, so the electrons should come out with more energy. In other words, the kinetic energy of the ejected electrons, \(K\), should be proportional to the intensity of the incident light, \(I_{\text{in}}\):
\[
K= c_{\text{PE}} \; I_{\text{in}},
\tag{2.4}\]
with \(c_{\text{PE}}\) being a constant that depends on the metal and on the characteristics of the incident light. The same picture also makes two other predictions: any color of light should be able to eject electrons, provided that it is bright enough, and with a very dim light the electrons should come out only after some delay, the time necessary to accumulate enough energy.
The experiments contradicted all three predictions. The kinetic energy of the ejected electrons does not depend on the intensity of the light at all (a brighter light ejects more electrons, but not faster ones), while it increases with the frequency of the light. Below a certain threshold frequency, which depends on the metal, no electrons are ejected, no matter how bright the light is. Above the threshold, electrons are ejected immediately, even with very dim light.
Einstein explained these results by proposing that a beam of light is not a continuous wave, but a stream of discrete packets of energy, the photons. The energy of each photon is equal to the smallest possible energy quantum in Planck’s theory of the black body (corresponding to \(n=1\) in Eq. 2.2):
\[
E = h \nu.
\tag{2.5}\]
Each photon interacts with a single electron, and gives it all of its energy at once. If the energy of the photon is smaller than the energy required to remove an electron from the metal, called the work function, \(\phi\), the electron cannot escape, and since there is no way of accumulating the energy of several photons, increasing the intensity (i.e., the number of photons) does not help. If the energy of the photon is larger than the work function, the electron escapes immediately, and the extra energy becomes its kinetic energy. The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons, \(K_{\text{max}}\), is therefore:
\[
K_{\text{max}} = E_{\text{in}} - \phi = h\nu_{\text{in}} - \phi,
\tag{2.6}\]
which depends on the frequency of the light, but not on its intensity, in agreement with the experiments. Eq. 2.6 is plotted for three metals in Fig. 2.2. For each metal, \(K_\text{max}\) is zero up to the threshold frequency, \(\nu_0=\phi/h\), and then increases linearly with the frequency. The lines for all metals are parallel, since their slope is always the Planck constant, \(h\). In 1916, Robert Millikan measured these lines very carefully, confirming Einstein’s prediction and obtaining a value of \(h\) in agreement with Planck’s. Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for this explanation.






Figure 2.2: Maximum kinetic energy of the electrons ejected from three metals as a function of the frequency of the light, according to the photoelectric equation. The threshold frequencies are marked with purple dots, and the shaded region is the visible part of the spectrum. Work functions are approximate.



For example, the work function of sodium is about \(2.3\;\text{eV}\).1 The threshold wavelength is \(\lambda_0=hc/\phi\approx1240/2.3\approx540\;\text{nm}\), so green, blue, and violet light can eject electrons from sodium, but yellow and red light cannot, no matter how bright. Ultraviolet light with \(\lambda=250\;\text{nm}\) carries photons of \(4.96\;\text{eV}\), and ejects electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of \(4.96-2.3\approx2.7\;\text{eV}\), corresponding to a speed of about \(10^6\;\text{m/s}\).

2.3.1 Why chemists care about photons
The energy of a single photon looks tiny in joules, but chemists usually think in terms of moles. A photon of green light (\(\lambda=500\;\text{nm}\)) has an energy of \(E=hc/\lambda=3.97\times10^{-19}\;\text{J}\), or \(2.48\;\text{eV}\). A mole of such photons carries \(3.97\times10^{-19}\;\text{J}\times6.022\times10^{23}\;\text{mol}^{-1}\approx239\;\text{kJ/mol}\). This is the same order of magnitude as the energy of a chemical bond (a \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}\) single bond is about \(350\;\text{kJ/mol}\)). Ultraviolet photons (\(\lambda=250\;\text{nm}\), \(479\;\text{kJ/mol}\)) carry enough energy to break chemical bonds, which is why UV light causes sunburns and can be used to sterilize surfaces, while visible photons can only excite electrons in molecules (which is how our eyes, and photosynthesis, work), and infrared photons can only make molecules vibrate. The interaction between light and molecules, one photon at a time, is the basis of spectroscopy, which we will discuss in Chapter 13.






Example 2.1: The photoelectric effect in sodium





Ultraviolet light with a wavelength of \(250\;\text{nm}\) shines on a sodium surface (work function \(\Phi=2.3\;\text{eV}\)). What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons?
Step 1: energy of one photon.
\[
E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{(6.626\times10^{-34}\;\text{J s})(2.998\times10^{8}\;\text{m/s})}{250\times10^{-9}\;\text{m}}=7.95\times10^{-19}\;\text{J}=4.96\;\text{eV}.
\]
(Per mole of photons, this is \(7.95\times10^{-19}\;\text{J}\times6.022\times10^{23}\;\text{mol}^{-1}=479\;\text{kJ/mol}\), more than enough to break most chemical bonds.)
Step 2: subtract the work function. Each photon gives all its energy to one electron, and \(2.3\;\text{eV}\) of it is needed to remove the electron from the metal:
\[
K_{\text{max}}=h\nu-\Phi=4.96\;\text{eV}-2.3\;\text{eV}=2.7\;\text{eV}.
\]
Notice that doubling the intensity of the light would double the number of ejected electrons, but would not change this value.

section: 2.4 Atomic Spectra and the Bohr Model
text:
2.4 Atomic Spectra and the Bohr Model
The third failure of classical physics is the one that matters most for chemistry, since it concerns atoms themselves. When a gas of hydrogen atoms is heated or excited by an electric discharge, it emits light. If this light is passed through a prism, it does not produce a continuous rainbow, like the light from a black body, but a series of sharp lines, each with a precise wavelength. In the visible region, hydrogen emits only four lines: red (\(656\;\text{nm}\)), blue-green (\(486\;\text{nm}\)), violet (\(434\;\text{nm}\)), and deep violet (\(410\;\text{nm}\)). Every element has its own characteristic set of lines, which can be used to identify it, as a fingerprint (this is how helium was discovered in the spectrum of the Sun, before it was found on Earth).
In 1885, Johann Balmer found a simple formula that reproduces the wavelengths of the visible lines of hydrogen, and in 1888 Johannes Rydberg generalized it to all the lines of hydrogen, including those in the ultraviolet and infrared:
\[
\frac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right), \qquad n_2 > n_1,
\tag{2.7}\]
where \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are positive integers, and \(R_H=1.0968\times10^{7}\;\text{m}^{-1}\) is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen. The lines with \(n_1=1\) are in the ultraviolet (the Lyman series), those with \(n_1=2\) are mostly in the visible (the Balmer series), and those with \(n_1=3\) are in the infrared (the Paschen series). For example, for \(n_1=2\) and \(n_2=3\), Eq. 2.7 gives \(1/\lambda=R_H\cdot\frac{5}{36}\), or \(\lambda=656\;\text{nm}\), the red line of hydrogen. The formula worked perfectly, but nobody knew why. Classical physics could not explain why atoms emit only certain wavelengths. Worse, as we mentioned at the beginning of this chapter, according to classical physics an electron orbiting a nucleus should continuously emit radiation of all wavelengths while spiraling into the nucleus.
In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model that explained the hydrogen spectrum by combining Rutherford’s nuclear atom with Planck’s idea of quantization. The Bohr model is based on two assumptions:

The electron moves around the nucleus only on certain circular orbits, called stationary states, on which it does not emit radiation. On these orbits, the angular momentum of the electron is quantized: it can only be a whole multiple of \(\hbar=h/2\pi\), \(L=n\hbar\), with \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\)
The atom emits or absorbs light only when the electron jumps from one orbit to another. The energy of the photon is equal to the difference between the energies of the two orbits, \(h\nu=E_{n_2}-E_{n_1}\).

Combining the first assumption with the classical laws of motion for an electron attracted by a proton (Coulomb’s law, Chapter 1), Bohr found that the allowed energies of the electron are:
\[
E_n = -\frac{m_e e^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2h^2}\frac{1}{n^2} = -\frac{13.6\;\text{eV}}{n^2}, \qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots
\tag{2.8}\]
and the radius of the smallest orbit, now called the Bohr radius, is \(a_0=0.529\;\text{Å}\). The energy levels of Eq. 2.8 and the transitions between them are shown in Fig. 2.3.






Figure 2.3: Top: energy levels of the hydrogen atom according to the Bohr model, and the transitions that produce the Lyman, Balmer, and Paschen series of emission lines. Bottom: the visible lines of the Balmer series, with their wavelengths in nm.



This diagram explains three features of atomic spectra:

Quantized energy levels explain line spectra: since the electron can only have the energies of Eq. 2.8, the photons emitted when it jumps from a higher level to a lower one can only have the energies \(E_{n_2}-E_{n_1}=13.6\;\text{eV}\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)\). Dividing by \(hc\) gives exactly the Rydberg formula, Eq. 2.7, with \(R_H=13.6\;\text{eV}/hc=1.097\times10^{7}\;\text{m}^{-1}\), in perfect agreement with the experimental value.
Ionization energy: the levels get closer and closer as \(n\) increases, and they converge to \(E=0\), which corresponds to the electron completely separated from the proton. The energy needed to remove the electron from the lowest level, \(13.6\;\text{eV}\) (or \(1{,}312\;\text{kJ/mol}\)), is the ionization energy of hydrogen, again in perfect agreement with experiments.
The meaning of the series: all lines of a series end on the same lower level. The Lyman series, which ends on \(n=1\), involves the largest energy jumps, and it is in the ultraviolet. The Balmer series, which ends on \(n=2\), involves smaller jumps, and its first lines are visible.

Despite this spectacular success, the Bohr model has serious problems. It works only for hydrogen and for ions with a single electron (such as \(\mathrm{He}^+\) and \(\mathrm{Li}^{2+}\)), and it fails already for the helium atom. It cannot explain the intensities of the lines, nor why some lines split in a magnetic field. Most importantly, it does not explain why angular momentum should be quantized, or why an electron on an orbit should not radiate: these are assumptions made to fit the data. As we will see in Chapter 5, the Schrödinger equation gives exactly the same energies as Eq. 2.8, but without any of these assumptions, and with a completely different picture of the electron, which is not a particle moving on an orbit, but a wave.

title: 2  The Failure of Classical Physics
text:
2.5 Wave-Particle Duality
If light is made of particles, these particles should also carry momentum, and Einstein showed that the momentum of a photon is:
\[
p = \frac{h}{\lambda}.
\tag{2.9}\]
We can see where this result comes from in two steps. First, combining \(E = h \nu\) for a photon with \(\lambda \nu = c\) for an electromagnetic wave, we obtain the energy of a photon as a function of its wavelength:
\[
E = \frac{h c}{\lambda}.
\tag{2.10}\]
Second, according to Einstein’s theory of relativity, the energy of a particle with no mass, such as a photon, is related to its momentum by \(E = pc\).2 Replacing this relation in Eq. 2.10 and solving for \(\lambda\) we obtain:
\[
\lambda = \frac{h}{p},
\tag{2.11}\]
which is equivalent to Eq. 2.9. Light, therefore, behaves as a wave in some experiments (it can be diffracted, and it has a wavelength) and as a particle in others (it comes in packets with energy \(h \nu\) and momentum \(h/\lambda\)). In 1924, Louis de Broglie made the bold suggestion that this dual behavior is not unique to light, and that matter should also behave like a wave, with a wavelength given by the same Eq. 2.11. In 1927, Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer confirmed de Broglie’s hypothesis by observing a diffraction pattern when they shot a beam of electrons at a nickel crystal, exactly as if the electrons were waves. We will discuss the wave behavior of electrons in more detail in Chapter 8.
Why don’t we notice the wave nature of everyday objects? Because \(h\) is so small. A baseball with a mass of \(0.145\text{ kg}\) thrown at \(40\text{ m/s}\) has a de Broglie wavelength of \(\lambda = h/mv \approx 1\times10^{-34}\text{ m}\), far too small to be observed in any experiment. An electron accelerated to a speed of \(10^6\text{ m/s}\), instead, has a wavelength of about \(7\times10^{-10}\text{ m}\), comparable to the size of an atom. This is why wave behavior dominates the world of electrons, atoms, and molecules, and why chemistry needs quantum mechanics.
Rewriting the previous equations in terms of the wave vector, \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\), and the angular frequency, \(\omega=2\pi\nu\), that we introduced in Chapter 1, we obtain the following two equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p &= \hbar k \\
E &= \hbar \omega,
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.12}\]
which are known as de Broglie’s equations. We will use these equations to develop wave mechanics in the next chapter.

title: 2  The Failure of Classical Physics
text:
2.6 Summary
The four experiments discussed in this chapter, and the new ideas that they introduced, are summarized in Table 2.1.



Table 2.1: The experiments that led to quantum mechanics.











Experiment
Classical prediction
Observation
Quantum idea




Black-body radiation
Intensity grows without limit at short wavelengths
Intensity peaks and goes to zero at short wavelengths
Energy is exchanged in quanta, \(E=nh\nu\) (Planck, 1900)


Photoelectric effect
Electron energy grows with light intensity; any color works
Electron energy depends only on frequency; threshold frequency
Light is made of photons, \(E=h\nu\) (Einstein, 1905)


Atomic line spectra
Continuous emission; electrons spiral into the nucleus
Sharp lines at specific wavelengths; atoms are stable
Atoms have quantized energy levels (Bohr, 1913)


Electron diffraction
Electrons are particles and cannot interfere
Diffraction patterns, as for waves
Matter behaves as waves, \(\lambda=h/p\) (de Broglie, 1924)






The common thread of all these results is that, at the scale of atoms and molecules, energy is not continuous, and particles and waves are not separate categories. In the next chapter, we will see how Schrödinger combined these ideas into a single equation.

title: 2  The Failure of Classical Physics
text:
2.7 Chapter Review

2.7.1 Key Ideas

Black-body radiation could only be explained by assuming that energy is exchanged in quanta, \(E=h\nu\) (Planck).
The photoelectric effect showed that light is made of photons: the energy of the ejected electrons depends on the frequency of the light, not on its intensity.
The sharp lines of atomic spectra show that atoms have discrete energy levels. The Bohr model explained hydrogen, but not why quantization happens.
Particles behave as waves, with wavelength \(\lambda=h/p\) (de Broglie). The effect matters only for very light particles such as electrons.
At the scale of atoms, energy is not continuous, and particles and waves are not separate categories.



2.7.2 Study Questions
1. What did classical physics (the Rayleigh–Jeans law) predict for the radiation emitted by a black body?

the intensity peaks and then goes to zero at short wavelengths
the intensity grows without limit at short wavelengths
no radiation is emitted at room temperature
the intensity is the same at all wavelengths
only visible light is emitted


2. Which assumption did Planck introduce to explain black-body radiation?

light travels faster at short wavelengths
atoms have a nucleus
energy is exchanged only in multiples of \(h\nu\)
electrons are waves
energy is not conserved in the emission of light


3. As the temperature of a black body increases, the maximum of its emission:

moves to longer wavelengths
moves to shorter wavelengths
does not move
disappears
moves to longer wavelengths and becomes weaker


4. Light with a frequency below the threshold frequency shines on a metal. If we increase its intensity:

still no electrons are ejected
electrons are ejected with more kinetic energy
electrons are ejected after a short delay
more electrons are ejected, all with the same kinetic energy
the threshold frequency decreases


5. In the photoelectric effect, the kinetic energy of an ejected electron is:

proportional to the intensity of the light
\(K=h\nu+\Phi\)
\(K=h\nu-\Phi\), where \(\Phi\) is the work function of the metal
the same for all frequencies above the threshold
\(K=\Phi/h\nu\)


6. The energy of a single photon depends on:

the intensity of the light
the number of photons in the beam
the temperature of the source
its frequency only, \(E=h\nu\)
the size of the source


7. What do the sharp lines in the spectrum of hydrogen tell us?

that the electron spirals into the nucleus
that hydrogen emits light at all wavelengths
that light is a classical wave
that the hydrogen atom has many electrons
that the atom can only have certain discrete energies


8. Which of the following is a problem of the Bohr model?

it works only for atoms with one electron, and its assumptions have no justification
it cannot explain the lines of the hydrogen spectrum
it predicts that atoms are not stable
it gives the wrong value of the ionization energy of hydrogen
it does not use Planck’s constant


9. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum \(p\) is:

\(\lambda=hp\)
\(\lambda=p/h\)
\(\lambda=h\nu\)
\(\lambda=c/p\)
\(\lambda=h/p\)


10. Why don’t we observe the wave nature of a thrown baseball?

because a baseball has no momentum
because only charged particles have a wavelength
because a baseball moves faster than light
because its de Broglie wavelength is far smaller than any object or opening it could interact with
because its de Broglie wavelength is too long to be measured

1.b, 2.c, 3.b, 4.a, 5.c, 6.d, 7.e, 8.a, 9.e, 10.d

title: 2  The Failure of Classical Physics
text:
The electronvolt, eV, is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt: \(1\;\text{eV}=1.602\times10^{-19}\;\text{J}\). It is a convenient unit for the energies of single electrons and photons. A useful shortcut for photons is \(E(\text{eV})\approx1240/\lambda(\text{nm})\).↩︎
This might be surprising, since in classical mechanics momentum is \(p=mv\), and a particle without mass should have no momentum. In relativity, however, momentum and energy are more general concepts, and a massless particle that always travels at the speed of light can carry both. The fact that light carries momentum can be measured directly: light pushes on the objects that absorb or reflect it, a phenomenon called radiation pressure.↩︎

2  The Failure of Classical Physics

title: 3  The Schrödinger Equation
text:
3.1 The Time-Independent Schrödinger Equation
As we saw in the previous chapter, quantum mechanics was born in two different forms: Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics and Schrödinger’s wave mechanics. The two are mathematically equivalent, and we are free to start from either one. In this textbook, we start from Schrödinger’s version, because it is written in the language of waves and differential equations, which is closer to the physics and mathematics that chemistry students already know. Schrödinger’s main idea was simple: if matter behaves as a wave, as de Broglie had proposed, there should be a wave equation that describes it.
The Schrödinger equation cannot be derived from classical physics, since it contains new physics that classical physics does not have. We can, however, make it plausible, by combining the mathematical description of a classical wave with de Broglie’s relations. We start from the simplest wave that travels through space, the complex plane wave moving along \(x\) that we introduced in Sec. 1.3:
\[
\psi(x,t)=\exp[i(kx-\omega t)],
\tag{3.1}\]
where \(x\) is the position, \(t\) is time, \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\) is the wave vector, and \(\omega=2\pi\nu\) is the angular frequency of the wave. If we are not concerned with the time evolution, we can consider uniquely the derivatives of Eq. 3.1 with respect to the location, which are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} &=ik\exp[i(kx-\omega t)] = ik\psi, \\
\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x^2} &=i^2k^2\exp[i(kx-\omega t)] = -k^2\psi,
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2}\]
where we have used the fact that \(i^2=-1\).
Assuming that particles behave as waves—as proposed by de Broglie—we can now use the first of de Broglie’s equations, Eq. 2.12, to replace \(k=\frac{p}{\hbar}\) and obtain:
\[
\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x^2} = -\frac{p^2\psi}{\hbar^2},
\tag{3.3}\]
which can be rearranged to:
\[
p^2 \psi = -\hbar^2 \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x^2}.
\tag{3.4}\]
The total energy associated with a wave moving in space is simply the sum of its kinetic and potential energies:
\[
E = \frac {p^{2}}{2m} + V(x),
\tag{3.5}\]
from which we can obtain:
\[
p^2 = 2m[E - V(x)],
\tag{3.6}\]
which we can then replace into Eq. 3.4 to obtain:
\[
2m[E-V(x)]\psi = - \hbar^2 \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x^2},
\tag{3.7}\]
which can then be rearranged to the famous time-independent Schrödinger equation (TISEq):
\[
- \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x^2} + V(x) \psi = E\psi,
\tag{3.8}\]
Remember that we did not prove this equation: we only showed that it is consistent with a plane wave and with de Broglie’s relations. Its real justification is that its predictions agree with experiments, as we will see in the following chapters. Notice also that the equation describes a single particle of mass \(m\). If we want to describe the relative motion of two particles, such as the two atoms in a diatomic molecule or the electron and the proton in a hydrogen atom, we can use the same equation, as long as we replace \(m\) with the reduced mass of the two particles, \(\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1+m_2}\).

text:
3.2 The Meaning of the Wave Function
We now have an equation for the wave function, but we have not yet said what the wave function is. Unlike the displacement of a guitar string or the electric field of a light wave, the wave function of a particle is not something that we can measure directly. It is, in general, a complex function, so it cannot itself be a measurable quantity. Its physical meaning was proposed by Max Born in 1926, and it is known as Born’s interpretation: the square magnitude of the wave function gives the probability of finding the particle at a given position. More precisely, for a particle moving along \(x\):
\[
\text{probability of finding the particle between } x \text{ and } x+dx = |\psi(x)|^2\,dx,
\tag{3.9}\]
where \(|\psi(x)|^2=\psi^*(x)\psi(x)\) is called the probability density. Notice that, even if \(\psi\) is complex, \(\psi^*\psi\) is always real and never negative, as a probability must be. This is similar to what happens for classical waves (Chapter 1), where the energy carried by a wave depends on the square of its amplitude, and not on the amplitude itself. For this reason, the wave function is sometimes called a probability amplitude.
Since the particle must be found somewhere, the probabilities of finding it at all possible positions must add up to one:
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |\psi(x)|^2\,dx = 1.
\tag{3.10}\]
This requirement is called the normalization condition, and a wave function that satisfies it is said to be normalized. For a particle moving in three dimensions, the integral runs over all three coordinates, \(\int |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2\,d\mathbf{r}=1\). If we multiply a solution of the Schrödinger equation by any constant, we still have a solution, so the normalization condition is what fixes the overall size of the wave function. We will see how this works in practice for the particle in a box in Chapter 4.
The probabilistic interpretation is one of the most radical departures of quantum mechanics from classical physics. A classical particle has a definite position at every moment; a quantum particle, instead, is described by a wave function that tells us only how likely it is to be found at each position. We will come back to the consequences of this idea, which still puzzle physicists and philosophers, in Chapter 8.






Example 3.1: Normalizing a wave function





A particle confined between \(x=0\) and \(x=a\) is described by \(\psi(x)=N\,x(a-x)\) inside this region and \(\psi=0\) outside. Find the normalization constant \(N\).
Step 1: write the normalization condition. Since \(\psi\) is real, \(|\psi|^2=\psi^2\):
\[
\int_0^a N^2x^2(a-x)^2\,dx = 1.
\]
Step 2: expand and integrate. \(x^2(a-x)^2=a^2x^2-2ax^3+x^4\), so:
\[
\int_0^a \left(a^2x^2-2ax^3+x^4\right)dx=\frac{a^5}{3}-\frac{2a^5}{4}+\frac{a^5}{5}=\frac{a^5}{30}.
\]
Step 3: solve for \(N\). \(N^2\,a^5/30=1\), so \(N=\sqrt{30/a^5}\).
Notice that the units work out: \(N\) has units of \((\text{length})^{-5/2}\), so that \(|\psi|^2\) has units of \((\text{length})^{-1}\), as a probability per unit length should.

text:
3.3 The Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation
The argument that we used in the previous section does not work for the time dependence of the wave function. Historically, Schrödinger also published the time-independent equation first, and only later proposed the more general time-dependent one. We will follow the same order, and simply state the time-dependent equation without derivation, as a basic assumption of the theory, whose justification is that its predictions agree with experiments. For a single particle moving in one dimension, the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSEq) is:
\[
i\hbar\frac{\partial \psi(x,t)}{\partial t}=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2 \psi(x,t)}{\partial x^2}+V(x)\psi(x,t)
\tag{3.11}\]
where \(V(x)\) is the potential energy of the system, which we assume does not depend on time. The TISEq is a special case of this equation. To see how, we try a wave function written as the product of a function of position and a function of time, \(\psi(x, t) = \psi(x) f(t)\). Replacing it into Eq. 3.11, we obtain:
\[
\psi(x) i \hbar \frac{df(t)}{dt} = f(t) \left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} + V(x) \right] \psi(x),
\tag{3.12}\]
which can be rearranged to:
\[
\frac{i \hbar}{f(t)} \frac{df(t)}{dt} = \frac{1}{\psi(x)} \left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} + V(x) \right] \psi(x).
\tag{3.13}\]
The left-hand side of Eq. 3.13 depends only on \(t\), and the right-hand side only on \(x\). The only way for the two to be equal for every value of \(x\) and \(t\) is for both of them to be equal to the same constant. The right-hand side has the dimensions of energy, so we call this constant \(E\). We have now split one partial differential equation into two ordinary differential equations:
\[
\frac{1}{f(t)} \frac{df(t)}{dt} = - \frac{i E}{\hbar}
\tag{3.14}\]
and: \[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2\psi(x)}{\partial x^2} + V(x) \psi(x) =
E \psi(x).
\tag{3.15}\]
The second equation is the TISEq that we obtained in the previous section. The first one is easy to solve, giving:
\[
f(t) = e^{-iEt / \hbar}
\tag{3.16}\]
This function oscillates in time, but its magnitude is always equal to one. Therefore, if the wave function is:
\[
\psi(x, t) = \psi(x) \exp\left(\frac{-iEt}{\hbar}\right),
\tag{3.17}\]
then \(\psi(x, t)\) differs from \(\psi(x)\) only by a phase factor that rotates in the complex plane without changing its size. As a consequence, the quantity \(\vert \psi(x, t) \vert^2\) does not depend on time:
\[
\vert \psi(x, t) \vert^2 = \psi^{*}(x, t) \psi(x, t)=
\psi^{*}(x)\exp\left(\frac{iEt}{\hbar}\right)\psi(x)\exp\left(\frac{-iEt}{\hbar}\right)= \psi^{*}(x) \psi(x).
\tag{3.18}\]
Wave functions of the form of Eq. 3.17 are called stationary states. As we saw in Sec. 3.2, \(\vert \psi(x, t) \vert^2\) is a probability density, the quantity that we can measure, so in a stationary state nothing that we can observe changes in time. This does not mean that the particle is standing still, but only that its probability distribution does not change. This is why the solutions of the TISEq are so important: they are the states with a well-defined energy, and they do not change in time. Not every solution of the TDSEq is a stationary state, but every solution can be written as a linear combination (a superposition) of stationary states:1
\[
\psi(\mathbf{r}, t) = \sum_i c_i e^{-iE_it / \hbar} \psi_i(\mathbf{r}).
\tag{3.19}\]

text:
3.5 Chapter Review

3.5.1 Key Ideas

The Schrödinger equation, \(\hat{H}\psi=E\psi\), cannot be derived from classical physics; it is justified by its agreement with experiments.
The wave function itself is not observable: \(|\psi|^2\) is a probability density (Born’s interpretation), and the total probability must be one (normalization).
Stationary states have a definite energy, and their probability density does not change in time.
A free particle with a definite momentum is a plane wave, equally likely to be anywhere. Its energy is not quantized.
A localized particle is a wave packet, a superposition of plane waves with a range of momenta: localization in space requires uncertainty in momentum.



3.5.2 Study Questions
1. Which of the following is the time-independent Schrödinger equation for a particle in one dimension?

\(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d\psi}{dx}+V(x)\psi=E\psi\)
\(\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2}=V(x)\)
\(m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\frac{dV}{dx}\)
\(\psi=E\,V(x)\)
\(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2}+V(x)\psi=E\psi\)


2. How was the Schrödinger equation obtained?

it cannot be derived from classical physics; we can make it plausible, and it is justified by its agreement with experiments
it was derived from Newton’s equation
it was derived from Coulomb’s law
it was obtained by measuring wave functions
it was derived from the Bohr model


3. According to Born’s interpretation, \(|\psi(x)|^2dx\) is:

the energy of the particle at \(x\)
the charge of the particle
the fraction of the particle located at \(x\)
the probability of finding the particle between \(x\) and \(x+dx\)
the velocity of the particle at \(x\)


4. Why must a wave function be normalized, \(\int|\psi|^2dx=1\)?

because the energy must be positive
because the particle must be found somewhere
because the wave function must be real
because the particle cannot move
because \(\psi\) must be zero everywhere


5. Why do we always use \(|\psi|^2=\psi^*\psi\), and not \(\psi\) itself, to compute probabilities?

because \(\psi\) can be complex, while \(\psi^*\psi\) is always real and never negative
because \(\psi\) is always negative
because \(\psi^*\psi\) is always larger than \(\psi\)
because \(\psi\) has no units
because \(\psi^*\psi\) is easier to differentiate


6. For a stationary state, what does not change in time?

the wave function \(\psi(x,t)\)
the phase of the wave function
the probability density \(|\psi(x,t)|^2\)
the real part of the wave function
nothing: everything changes in time


7. A stationary state with energy \(E\) evolves in time by multiplication with which factor?

\(e^{-Et/\hbar}\)
\(\cos(Et)\)
\(e^{iEx/\hbar}\)
\(e^{-iEt/\hbar}\)
\(E\,t\)


8. The energy of a free particle is:

\(E=\frac{p^2}{2m}\), but only integer multiples of \(h\nu\)
\(E=\frac{p^2}{2m}\), and it can take any non-negative value
always zero
\(E=mc^2\)
\(E=\frac{n^2h^2}{8ma^2}\)


9. A particle described by a single plane wave, \(\psi=e^{ikx}\), has:

a perfectly defined position, but undefined momentum
a perfectly defined position and momentum
zero momentum
a probability density that oscillates with \(x\)
a perfectly defined momentum, but the same probability of being found anywhere


10. To describe a particle localized in a small region of space, we need:

a single plane wave with a very large momentum
a single plane wave with zero momentum
a wave packet, a superposition of plane waves with a range of momenta
a wave function equal to zero everywhere
a classical trajectory








ExampleAnswers





1.e, 2.a, 3.d, 4.b, 5.a, 6.c, 7.d, 8.b, 9.e, 10.c

title: 4  Analytically Solvable Models
text:
4.1 The Particle in a Box
The TISEq can be solved analytically only in a few special cases. We saw one of those special cases, the free particle, at the end of the previous chapter. In this chapter, we will analyze four others. Luckily, we can use these solutions to explain most of the effects in chemistry since we can combine them to describe the hydrogen atom upon which we can build more complex chemical systems, as we will show in the next chapters.
We can start by considering a particle constrained to move in a single dimension, under the influence of a potential \(V(x)\) which is zero for \(0 \leq x \leq a\) and infinite elsewhere. Since the wavefunction is not allowed to become infinite, it must have a value of zero where \(V(x)\) is infinite, so \(\psi(x)\) is nonzero only within \([0,a]\). The Schrödinger equation is thus:
\[
- \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} = E \psi(x)
\qquad 0 \leq x \leq a.
\tag{4.1}\]
In other words, inside the box \(\psi(x)\) describes a free particle, but outside the box \(\psi(x)=0\). Since the Schrödinger equation involves derivatives, the function that solves it, \(\psi(x)\), must be everywhere continuous. This fact means that the value of the wave function at the two extremes must be equal to zero:
\[
\psi(0)=\psi(a)=0.
\tag{4.2}\]
Inside the box the solution will be the same as for the free particle:
\[
\psi(x) = A e^{ikx} + B e^{-ikx},
\tag{4.3}\]
where \(A\) and \(B\) are constants. Using the two constraints in Eq. 4.2, we get at \(x=0\):
\[
\psi(0) = A + B = 0 \implies B = -A
\tag{4.4}\]
And at \(x=a\):
\[
\psi(a) = A e^{ika} + B e^{-ika} = 0.
\tag{4.5}\]
Replacing Eq. 4.4 into Eq. 4.5 gives:
\[
A e^{ika} - A e^{-ika} = 0
\tag{4.6}\]
which is then easily simplified into:
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{ika} &= e^{-ika}\\
e^{i2ka} &= 1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.7}\]
This equation is solved when:
\[
2ka = 2n\pi,
\tag{4.8}\]
which is trivially solved for \(n=0\), giving either \(k=0\) or \(a=0\). This trivial solution is completely uninteresting, since it describes no particles in no boxes. A more interesting set of solutions however, are those for which:
\[
k_n = \frac{n\pi}{a} \quad (n = 1, 2, 3,\dots,\infty),
\tag{4.9}\]
which represents an infinite set of functions, \(\psi_n(x)\), determined by a positive integer number \(n\), called quantum number. Since these functions solve the TISEq, they are also called eigenfunctions, but they are not a continuous set, unlike in the previous case.
Using Eq. 4.4, the wave functions become:
\[
\psi_n(x) = A \left(e^{i\frac{n\pi x}{a}} - e^{-i\frac{n\pi x}{a}}\right),
\tag{4.10}\]
and using Euler’s formula \(\left(\sin\theta = \frac{e^{i\theta} - e^{-i\theta}}{2i}\right)\), we get:
\[
\psi_n(x) = 2iA \frac{e^{i\frac{n\pi x}{a}} - e^{-i\frac{n\pi x}{a}}}{2i} = C \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{a}\right)
\tag{4.11}\]
where \(C = 2iA\) is a complex constant.
To calculate the energy eigenvalues, we can replace Eq. 4.11 into Eq. 4.1, to obtain:
\[
E_n = n^2 \frac{\pi^2 \hbar^2 }{2 m a^2} = \frac{n^2 h^2}{8 m a^2} \quad (n=1,2,\ldots,\infty).
\tag{4.12}\]
Eq. 4.12 tells us a few interesting things. First, although there is an infinite number of acceptable values of the energy (eigenvalues), these values are not continuous. Second, the lowest value of the energy is not zero, and it depends on the size of the box, \(a\), since:
\[
E_1 = \frac{\pi^2 \hbar^2 }{2 m a^2}\neq 0.
\tag{4.13}\]
This value is called zero-point energy (ZPE), and is a purely quantum mechanical effect. Notice that we have not determined the constant \(C\) yet. We will do so in a moment, using the normalization condition of Chapter 3.
The most profound physical insight from the particle in a box solution comes from applying Born’s interpretation of the wave function (Sec. 3.2). The probability of finding the particle in state \(n\) between positions \(x\) and \(x+dx\) is \(|\psi_n(x)|^2 dx\), so the probability densities \(|\psi_n(x)|^2\) tell us where the particle is likely to be found inside the box.
Since the particle must be somewhere inside the box, the probability of finding it anywhere between \(x=0\) and \(x=a\) must be equal to one. This is the normalization condition, Eq. 3.10, with the integral limited to the inside of the box (outside, the wave function is zero), and it is exactly what we need to determine the constant \(C\):
\[
\int_0^a |\psi_n(x)|^2\, dx = |C|^2 \int_0^a \sin^2\left(\frac{n\pi x}{a}\right) dx = 1.
\tag{4.14}\]
Using the trigonometric identity \(\sin^2\theta = \frac{1 - \cos(2\theta)}{2}\), the integral becomes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^a \sin^2\left(\frac{n\pi x}{a}\right) dx &= \frac{1}{2}\int_0^a dx - \frac{1}{2}\int_0^a \cos\left(\frac{2n\pi x}{a}\right) dx \\
&= \frac{a}{2} - \frac{a}{4n\pi}\Big[\sin\left(\frac{2n\pi x}{a}\right)\Big]_0^a = \frac{a}{2},
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.15}\]
since the sine vanishes at both limits. Replacing this result into Eq. 4.14 gives \(|C|^2\frac{a}{2}=1\), or \(|C|=\sqrt{\frac{2}{a}}\). Only the magnitude of \(C\) is fixed by this condition, and we can choose it to be real and positive. The normalized eigenfunctions of the particle in a box are therefore:
\[
\psi_n(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{a}}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{a}\right) \quad (n=1,2,\ldots,\infty).
\tag{4.16}\]
Notice that the normalization constant is the same for every \(n\), and that it depends only on the size of the box: the larger the box, the more the probability is spread out, and the smaller the amplitude of the wave function. The same condition applies to any system: since the probability of finding the particle somewhere in space must be one, every acceptable wave function must satisfy \(\int |\psi|^2\, d\tau = 1\), where the integral runs over all the coordinates of the system. The probabilistic interpretation also puts some restrictions on what an acceptable wave function can look like. It must be single-valued, since the probability of finding the particle at a given point cannot have two different values. It must be continuous (and, where the potential is finite, so must be its first derivative), since the TISEq contains its second derivative. And it must be finite everywhere, and go to zero at large distances fast enough for the normalization integral to exist. We already used these conditions when we required the wave function to vanish at the walls of the box, and we will use them again for every system in this textbook.
For the particle in a box eigenfunctions in Eq. 4.11, the probability density is:
\[
|\psi_n(x)|^2 = |C|^2 \sin^2\left(\frac{n\pi x}{a}\right).
\tag{4.17}\]
This function tells us where the particle is most likely to be found if we measure its position.
