title: 6  Operators, Observables, and Measurements
text:
6.5 Chapter Review

6.5.1 Key Ideas

Every observable is represented by a Hermitian operator. The possible results of a measurement are its eigenvalues, which are always real.
The expectation value, \(\langle A\rangle=\int\psi^*\hat{A}\psi\,d\mathbf{r}\), is the average of many measurements on identically prepared systems.
For a superposition of eigenfunctions, each eigenvalue is measured with probability \(|c_i|^2\).
Operators that commute share eigenfunctions, and their observables can have definite values together. Position and momentum do not commute: \([\hat{x},\hat{p}]=i\hbar\).
The Hamiltonian determines the time evolution. Superpositions of states with different energies change in time, with frequencies \((E_2-E_1)/h\).



6.5.2 Study Questions
1. If we measure an observable \(A\) on a system, the possible results are:

any real number
the eigenfunctions of \(\hat{A}\)
the eigenvalues of the operator \(\hat{A}\)
only the expectation value \(\langle A\rangle\)
the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian, whatever \(A\) is


2. The expectation value \(\langle A\rangle\) is:

the result of a single measurement
the largest possible result of a measurement
always an eigenvalue of \(\hat{A}\)
the uncertainty in the measurement of \(A\)
the average of the results of many measurements of \(A\) on identically prepared systems


3. For a normalized wave function \(\psi\), the expectation value of \(\hat{A}\) is:

\(\langle A\rangle=\int\hat{A}\psi\,d\mathbf{r}\)
\(\langle A\rangle=\int\psi^*\hat{A}\psi\,d\mathbf{r}\)
\(\langle A\rangle=\int\psi^*\psi\,d\mathbf{r}\)
\(\langle A\rangle=\hat{A}\psi\)
\(\langle A\rangle=\int\psi\hat{A}\,d\mathbf{r}\)


4. Why are the operators associated with observables Hermitian?

because Hermitian operators always commute with each other
because Hermitian operators are always real
because Hermitian operators have no eigenfunctions
because Hermitian operators have real eigenvalues, and the results of measurements are real numbers
because Hermitian operators do not depend on position


5. Eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator with different eigenvalues are:

orthogonal
identical
always degenerate
complex conjugates of each other
normalized to zero


6. A system is described by \(\psi=c_1\psi_a+c_2\psi_b\), where \(\psi_a\) and \(\psi_b\) are normalized eigenfunctions of \(\hat{A}\) with eigenvalues \(a\) and \(b\). A measurement of \(A\) gives:

always \(c_1a+c_2b\)
always \(a\), the lowest eigenvalue
\(a\) and \(b\) at the same time
\(a\) with probability \(|c_1|^2\), or \(b\) with probability \(|c_2|^2\)
\(a\) with probability \(c_1\), or \(b\) with probability \(c_2\)


7. In one dimension, the momentum operator is:

\(\hat{p}=-i\hbar\frac{d}{dx}\)
\(\hat{p}=m\frac{dx}{dt}\)
\(\hat{p}=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\)
\(\hat{p}=x\)
\(\hat{p}=i\hbar x\)


8. The commutator of position and momentum is \([\hat{x},\hat{p}]=i\hbar\). This means that:

position and momentum can always be measured together exactly
no wave function can have a definite position and a definite momentum at the same time
momentum is always imaginary
position is quantized
the momentum of a particle is always zero


9. If two operators commute, \([\hat{A},\hat{B}]=0\):

they have the same eigenvalues
one of them must be the Hamiltonian
they have a common set of eigenfunctions, and both observables can have definite values at the same time
their observables cannot be measured
their eigenfunctions are always orthogonal to each other


10. A particle in a box is in a superposition of the two lowest energy eigenstates. Its probability density:

does not change in time
decays to zero
oscillates with frequency \(\nu=E_1/h\)
is the same everywhere in the box
oscillates back and forth with frequency \(\nu=(E_2-E_1)/h\)

title: 7  Spin
text:
7.1 Stern-Gerlach Experiment
Spin is a special property of particles that has no classical analogue. Spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum carried by elementary particles, such as the electron.
In 1922, Otto Stern and Walter Gerlach performed an experiment that unintentionally led to the discovery that electrons have their own intrinsic angular momentum (spin), independent of their orbital motion in an atom. The experiment was done by putting a silver foil in an oven to vaporize its atoms. The silver atoms were collected into a beam that passed through an inhomogeneous magnetic field. The result was that the magnetic field split the beam into two (and only two) separate ones. The Stern–Gerlach experiment demonstrated that the spatial orientation of angular momentum is quantized into two components (up and down). Thus an atomic-scale system was shown to have intrinsically quantum properties. The experiment is normally conducted using electrically neutral particles such as silver atoms. This avoids the large deflection in the path of a charged particle moving through a magnetic field and allows spin-dependent effects to dominate. A schematic of the apparatus is shown in Fig. 7.1.
If the particle is treated as a classical spinning magnetic dipole, it will precess in a magnetic field because of the torque that the magnetic field exerts on the dipole. If it moves through a homogeneous magnetic field, the forces exerted on opposite ends of the dipole cancel each other out and the trajectory of the particle is unaffected. However, if the magnetic field is inhomogeneous then the force on one end of the dipole will be slightly greater than the opposing force on the other end, so that there is a net force which deflects the particle’s trajectory. If the particles were classical spinning objects, one would expect the distribution of their spin angular momentum vectors to be random and continuous. Each particle would be deflected by an amount proportional to its magnetic moment, producing some density distribution on the detector screen. Instead, the particles passing through the Stern–Gerlach apparatus are equally distributed among two possible values, with half of them ending up at an upper spot (“spin up”), and the other half at the lower spot (“spin down”). Since the particles are deflected by a magnetic field, spin is a magnetic property that is associated with some intrinsic form of angular momentum. As we saw in Chapter 6, the quantization of the angular momentum gives energy levels that are \((2\ell+1)\)-fold degenerate. Since along the direction of the magnet we observe only two possible eigenvalues for the spin, we conclude the following value for \(s\):
\[
2s+1=2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s=\frac{1}{2}.
\tag{7.1}\]
The Stern-Gerlach experiment proves that electrons are spin-\(\frac{1}{2}\) particles. These have only two possible spin angular momentum values measured along any axis, \(+\frac {\hbar }{2}\) or \(-\frac {\hbar }{2}\), a purely quantum mechanical phenomenon. Because its value is always the same, it is regarded as an intrinsic property of electrons, and is sometimes known as “intrinsic angular momentum” (to distinguish it from orbital angular momentum, which can vary and depends on the presence of other particles).
The act of observing (measuring) the spin angular momentum along the \(z\) direction corresponds to the operator \(\hat{S}_z\), which projects the value of the total spin operator \(\hat{S}^2\) along the \(z\) axis. The eigenvalue equation for this projection operator is:
\[
\hat{S}_z \chi = \hbar m_s \chi,
\tag{7.2}\]
where \(m_s=\left\{-s,+s\right\}=\left\{-\frac{1}{2},+\frac{1}{2}\right\}\) is the spin quantum number along the \(z\) component. The eigenvalues for the total spin operator \(\hat{S}^2\)—similarly to the angular momentum operator \(\hat{L}^2\) seen in Eq. 6.27—are:
\[
\hat{S}^2 \chi = \hbar^2 s(s+1) \chi,
\tag{7.3}\]
Notice that the magnitude of the spin angular momentum, \(|\mathbf{S}|=\hbar\sqrt{s(s+1)}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar\approx0.87\hbar\), is larger than its largest possible projection on the \(z\) axis, \(\frac{1}{2}\hbar\). In other words, the spin vector can never point exactly along \(z\). A common way of picturing this result, shown in Fig. 7.2, is to imagine the spin vector lying somewhere on the surface of a cone around the \(z\) axis: its \(z\) component is well defined (\(+\frac{\hbar}{2}\) for \(\alpha\), and \(-\frac{\hbar}{2}\) for \(\beta\)), while its \(x\) and \(y\) components are not. As we will see in the next sections, this is a consequence of the fact that the three components of spin cannot be measured at the same time.
The initial state of the particles in the Stern-Gerlach experiment is given by the following wave function:
\[
\chi = c_1\, \alpha + c_2 \,\beta,
\tag{7.4}\]
where \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are the two eigenfunctions of \(\hat{S}_z\), corresponding to spin up (\(\uparrow\), \(m_s=+\frac{1}{2}\), eigenvalue \(+\frac{\hbar}{2}\)) and spin down (\(\downarrow\), \(m_s=-\frac{1}{2}\), eigenvalue \(-\frac{\hbar}{2}\)), respectively, and the coefficients \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are complex numbers. The names \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) for the two spin functions are standard in chemistry, and we will use them for the rest of this textbook. In this initial state, spin can point in any direction. The expectation value of the operator \(\hat{S}_z\) (the quantity that the Stern-Gerlach experiment measures), can be obtained using Eq. 6.20:
\[
\begin{aligned}
<S_z> &= \int \chi^{*} \hat{S}_z \chi \, d\mathbf{s} \\
&= +\frac{\hbar}{2} \vert c_1\vert^2 -\frac{\hbar}{2} \vert c_2\vert^2,
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.5}\]
where the integration is performed along a special coordinate \(\mathbf{s}\) composed of only two values. Applying the normalization condition, Eq. 6.18, we can obtain:
\[
|c_{1}|^{2}+|c_{2}|^{2}=1 \quad\longrightarrow\quad |c_{1}|^{2}=|c_{2}|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
\tag{7.6}\]
This equation is not sufficient to determine the values of the coefficients since they are complex numbers. Eq. 7.6, however, tells us that the squared magnitudes of the coefficients can be interpreted as probabilities of outcome from the experiment. This is true because their values are obtained from the normalization condition, and the normalization condition guarantees that the system is observed with probability equal to one. Summarizing, since we started with random initial directions, each of the two states, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), will be observed with equal probability of \(\frac{1}{2}\).

A beam of silver atoms from an oven is collimated by two slits and passes between the poles of a magnet shaped to produce an inhomogeneous field. The spin vector has length \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar\) and a well-defined projection on the \(z\) axis, \(+\frac{\hbar}{2}\) (\(\alpha\), red) or \(-\frac{\hbar}{2}\) (\(\beta\), blue), but its direction around the cone (i.e., its \(x\) and \(y\) components) is undetermined. The lighter arrows show other possible orientations on the same cone.
















Example 7.1: Spin probabilities





An electron is described by the spin function \(\chi=\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\alpha+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\beta\). What are the probabilities of measuring spin up and spin down along \(z\), and what is \(\langle S_z\rangle\)?
Step 1: check the normalization. \(\left|\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right|^2+\left|\tfrac{1}{2}\right|^2=\tfrac{3}{4}+\tfrac{1}{4}=1\).
Step 2: probabilities. \(P(\uparrow)=\tfrac{3}{4}\) and \(P(\downarrow)=\tfrac{1}{4}\).
Step 3: expectation value. Each result is weighted by its probability:
\[
\langle S_z\rangle=\tfrac{3}{4}\left(+\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\right)+\tfrac{1}{4}\left(-\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\right)=+\tfrac{\hbar}{4}.
\]
As for any superposition, a single measurement gives either \(+\hbar/2\) or \(-\hbar/2\), never \(\hbar/4\).

text:
7.2 Sequential Stern-Gerlach Experiments
An interesting result can be obtained if we link multiple Stern–Gerlach apparatuses into one experiment and we perform the measurement along two orthogonal directions in space. As we showed in the previous section, all particles leaving the first Stern-Gerlach apparatus are in an eigenstate of the \(\hat{S}_z\) operator (i.e., their spin is either “up” or “down” with respect to the \(z\)-direction). We can then take either one of the two resulting beams (for simplicity let’s take the “spin up” output), and perform another spin measurement on it. If the second measurement is also aligned along the \(z\)-direction then only one outcome will be measured, since all particles are already in the “spin up” eigenstate of \(\hat{S}_z\). In other words, the measurement of a particle being in an eigenstate of the corresponding operator leaves the state unchanged. The possible combinations of sequential experiments discussed in this section are summarized in Fig. 7.3.






Figure 7.3: Sequential Stern–Gerlach experiments, with the number of particles in each beam. (a) A single apparatus along \(z\) splits a beam of \(N\) particles into two equal beams. (b) A second apparatus along \(z\) does not split the spin-up beam any further. (c) An apparatus along \(x\) splits the spin-up beam into two beams, spin right and spin left; a third apparatus along \(z\) then splits the spin-right beam again into spin up and spin down, as if the first measurement had never happened.



If, however, we perform the spin measurement along a direction perpendicular to the original \(z\)-axis (i.e., the \(x\)-axis) then the output will equally distribute among “spin up” or ”spin down” in the \(x\)-direction, which in order to avoid confusion, we can call “spin left” and “spin right”. Thus, even though we knew the state of the particles beforehand, in this case the measurement resulted in a random spin flip in either of the measurement directions. Mathematically, this property is expressed by the nonvanishing of the commutator of the spin operators:
\[
\left[\hat{S}_z,\hat{S}_x \right] \neq 0.
\tag{7.7}\]
We can finally repeat the measurement a third time, with the magnet aligned along the original \(z\)-direction. According to classical physics, after the second apparatus, we would expect to have one beam with characteristic “spin up” and “spin left”, and another with characteristic “spin up” and “spin right”. The outcome of the third measurement along the original \(z\)-axis should be one output with characteristic “spin up”, regardless of which beam the magnet is applied (since the “spin down” component should have been “filtered out” by the first experiment, and the “spin left” and “spin right” component should be filtered out by the third magnet). This is not what is observed. The output of the third measurement is—once again—two beams in the \(z\) direction, one with “spin up” characteristic and the other with “spin down”.
This experiment shows that spin is not a classical property. The Stern-Gerlach apparatus does not behave as a simple filter, selecting beams with one specific pre-determined characteristic. The second measurement along the \(x\) axis destroys the previous determination of the angular momentum in the \(z\) direction. This means that this property cannot be measured on two perpendicular directions at the same time.

text:
7.3 Spin Operators
The mathematics of quantum mechanics tells us that \(\hat{S}_z\) and \(\hat{S}_x\) do not commute. As we saw in Sec. 6.3.3, when two operators do not commute, in general there is no state in which both of the associated quantities have a definite value: they cannot be known at the same time.
In 3-dimensional space there are three directions that are orthogonal to each other \(\left\{x,y,z\right\}\). Thus, we can define a third spin projection operator along the \(y\) direction, \(\hat{S}_y\), corresponding to a new set of Stern-Gerlach experiments where the second magnet is oriented along a direction that is orthogonal to the two that we considered in the previous section. The total spin operator, \(\hat{S}^2\), can then be constructed similarly to the total angular momentum operator of Eq. 6.26, as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{S}^2 &=\hat{S}\cdot\hat{S}=\left(\mathbf{i}\hat{S}_x+\mathbf{j}\hat{S}_y+\mathbf{k}\hat{S}_z\right)\cdot\left(\mathbf{i}\hat{S}_x+\mathbf{j}\hat{S}_y+\mathbf{k}\hat{S}_z \right) \\
&=\hat{S}_x^2+\hat{S}_y^2+\hat{S}_z^2,
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.8}\]
with \(\left\{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\right\}\) the unit vectors in three-dimensional space.
Wolfgang Pauli explicitly derived the relationships between all three spin projection operators. Assuming the magnetic field along the \(z\) axis, Pauli’s relations can be written using simple equations involving the two possible eigenstates \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{S}_x \alpha =  \frac{\hbar}{2} \beta \qquad \hat{S}_y \alpha &=  \frac{\hbar}{2} i \beta \qquad \hat{S}_z \alpha =  \frac{\hbar}{2} \alpha \\
\hat{S}_x \beta =  \frac{\hbar}{2} \alpha \qquad \hat{S}_y \beta &=  - \frac{\hbar}{2} i \alpha \qquad \hat{S}_z \beta =  -\frac{\hbar}{2} \beta,
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.9}\]
where \(i\) is the imaginary unit (\(i^2=-1\)). In other words, for \(\hat{S}_z\) we have eigenvalue equations, while the remaining components have the effect of permuting state \(\alpha\) with state \(\beta\) after multiplication by suitable constants. We can use these equations, together with Eq. 6.7, to calculate the commutator for each pair of spin projection operators:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left[\hat{S}_x, \hat{S}_y\right] &= i\hbar\hat{S}_z \\
\left[\hat{S}_y, \hat{S}_z\right] &= i\hbar\hat{S}_x \\
\left[\hat{S}_z, \hat{S}_x\right] &= i\hbar\hat{S}_y,
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.10}\]
In words: no two components of the spin commute with each other, so, as we saw for position and momentum, no state can have definite values of two different components at the same time. This is exactly what the sequential Stern–Gerlach experiments showed.






NoteProof: the commutators of the spin components





The commutators in Eq. 7.10 follow from Pauli’s relations, Eq. 7.9, and the definition of commutator, Eq. 6.7. We apply both sides to \(\alpha\) (applying them to \(\beta\) gives the same result). For the first pair:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left[\hat{S}_x, \hat{S}_y\right] \alpha &= \hat{S}_x\hat{S}_y\alpha-\hat{S}_y\hat{S}_x\alpha \\
&= \hat{S}_x \left(\frac{\hbar}{2}i \beta \right)-\hat{S}_y \left(\frac{\hbar}{2} \beta \right) \\
&= \frac{\hbar}{2}i \left(\frac{\hbar}{2} \alpha \right)- \frac{\hbar}{2} \left(-\frac{\hbar}{2}i \alpha \right) \\
&= \left(\frac{\hbar^2}{4}+\frac{\hbar^2}{4}\right)i\alpha \\
&= \frac{\hbar^2}{2}i \alpha \\
&= i\hbar\hat{S}_z  \alpha
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.11}\]

text:
7.4 Operators Commuting with the Hamiltonian
We have now met several quantum numbers: \(n\) for the particle in a box, \(m_\ell\) for the particle on a ring, \(\ell\) and \(m_\ell\) for the particle on a sphere, \(n\), \(\ell\), and \(m_\ell\) for the hydrogen atom, and now \(m_s\) for spin. At first sight, they look like a random collection of labels, each one coming out of a different calculation. To conclude this chapter, let’s step back and see that they all have the same origin.
The key is the theorem that we discussed in Sec. 6.3.3: if an operator \(\hat{A}\) commutes with the Hamiltonian, \([\hat{H},\hat{A}]=0\), we can find wave functions that are eigenfunctions of both. Each of these wave functions then has a definite energy and a definite value of the observable \(A\), and we can use the eigenvalue of \(\hat{A}\) as a label for the state. Moreover, since \(\hat{A}\) commutes with \(\hat{H}\), which controls the time evolution (Sec. 6.4), this label does not change in time: the observable \(A\) is conserved. Physicists call such a label a good quantum number.
So, the question “which quantum numbers does a system have?” becomes “which operators commute with its Hamiltonian?”. And, as we will see in the examples below, the answer to this second question comes from the symmetry of the system: every time the system looks the same after some operation (a shift, a reflection, a rotation), there is an operator that commutes with \(\hat{H}\), and a quantum number that comes with it.

7.4.1 Free particle: shifts and momentum
A free particle feels no potential, so its Hamiltonian contains only the kinetic energy, \(\hat{H}=\hat{p}^2/2m\). Its symmetry is that space looks the same everywhere: if we shift the whole system by any distance, nothing changes. The operator associated with this symmetry is the momentum, and since \(\hat{H}\) contains only \(\hat{p}\), the two commute:
\[
[\hat{H}, \hat{p}] = 0.
\tag{7.12}\]
This is why the free-particle solutions of Chapter 3, the plane waves \(e^{ikx}\), have both a definite energy and a definite momentum, \(p=\hbar k\), and why we can label them with \(k\).


7.4.2 Particle in a box: no more momentum, but parity
Inside a box, the particle is still free, but the walls break the symmetry: if we shift the system, the walls move, and the problem changes. As a consequence, \(\hat{p}\) no longer commutes with \(\hat{H}\), and momentum is not a good quantum number. We can check this directly: the eigenfunctions of the particle in a box, \(\sin(n\pi x/a)\), are not eigenfunctions of \(\hat{p}=-i\hbar\frac{d}{dx}\), since the derivative turns a sine into a cosine. (Using Euler’s formula, each sine is a combination of two plane waves, one moving to the right and one to the left, with opposite momenta. A measurement of momentum would give either one, but the state does not have a definite momentum.)
Some symmetry, however, survives. If we place the box symmetrically, between \(-a/2\) and \(+a/2\), the system looks the same when we reflect it through its center, \(x\rightarrow-x\). The operator that performs this reflection is called the parity operator, \(\hat{\Pi}\):
\[
\hat{\Pi}\,\psi(x) = \psi(-x).
\tag{7.13}\]
Whenever the potential is symmetric, \(V(-x)=V(x)\), the Hamiltonian does not change under reflection, and it commutes with parity, \([\hat{H},\hat{\Pi}]=0\). The energy eigenfunctions can then be chosen to be eigenfunctions of parity too. Since reflecting twice brings us back to where we started, the only possible eigenvalues are \(+1\) and \(-1\):

Even functions are unchanged by the reflection, \(\psi(-x)=+\psi(x)\).
Odd functions change sign, \(\psi(-x)=-\psi(x)\).

As shown in Fig. 7.4, the states of the particle in a box alternate between even and odd as the energy increases. Parity is a simple label, but a very useful one: it is the origin of the \(g\) and \(u\) labels of molecular orbitals in Chapter 11, and of many selection rules in Chapter 13, since the integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval is zero (Sec. A.3).






Figure 7.4: The first four eigenfunctions of a particle in a box placed symmetrically between \(-a/2\) and \(+a/2\). Even states (red labels) are unchanged by the inversion \(x\rightarrow -x\) (reflection through the purple dashed line), and odd states (blue labels) change sign.





7.4.3 Particle on a ring and on a sphere: rotations and angular momentum
A particle on a ring looks the same if we rotate the ring by any angle around its axis, \(z\). The operator associated with rotations around \(z\) is the \(z\) component of the angular momentum, so:
\[
[\hat{H}, \hat{L}_z] = 0.
\tag{7.14}\]
This is why the solutions of the particle on a ring, \(e^{im_\ell\phi}\), have both a definite energy and a definite angular momentum, \(L_z=m_\ell\hbar\) (Chapter 4), and why we can label them with \(m_\ell\).
A particle on a sphere looks the same after a rotation around any axis. Its Hamiltonian commutes with all three components of the angular momentum, and therefore also with \(\hat{L}^2\). Since the components do not commute with each other (Chapter 6), we cannot use all of them as labels at the same time. The best we can do is to pick \(\hat{L}^2\) and one component, by convention \(\hat{L}_z\):
\[
[\hat{H}, \hat{L}^2] = 0, \qquad [\hat{H}, \hat{L}_z] = 0,
\tag{7.15}\]
which give the two quantum numbers \(\ell\) (from \(L^2=\hbar^2\ell(\ell+1)\)) and \(m_\ell\) (from \(L_z=\hbar m_\ell\)) of the spherical harmonics. There is one more consequence of the symmetry. Since the sphere has no preferred direction, the energy cannot depend on the orientation of the angular momentum, that is, on \(m_\ell\). This is why each level \(\ell\) is \((2\ell+1)\) times degenerate: the degeneracy is the rotational symmetry.


7.4.4 Hydrogen atom: one label more, and an extra degeneracy
The Coulomb potential of the hydrogen atom depends only on the distance from the nucleus, \(r\), so the atom has the same rotational symmetry as the sphere, and \(\hat{H}\) commutes with \(\hat{L}^2\) and \(\hat{L}_z\). Together with the energy itself, this gives the three labels \(n\), \(\ell\), and \(m_\ell\) of the hydrogen orbitals.
Rotational symmetry explains why the energy does not depend on \(m_\ell\). It does not explain, however, why the energy of hydrogen does not depend on \(\ell\) either, so that, for example, the \(2s\) and \(2p\) orbitals have the same energy (Chapter 5). This additional degeneracy is a special property of the \(1/r\) potential, which has a hidden symmetry that goes beyond simple rotations (its discussion is beyond the scope of this book). As soon as the potential is no longer exactly \(1/r\), as for an electron in a many-electron atom shielded by the others, this degeneracy disappears, and the \(2s\) and \(2p\) energies split (Chapter 9).


7.4.5 Spin: why it matters
The hydrogen Hamiltonian that we used does not contain spin at all, so it automatically commutes with \(\hat{S}^2\) and \(\hat{S}_z\). Each spatial state \((n,\ell,m_\ell)\) can therefore be combined with either spin function, \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\), giving a fourth label, \(m_s=\pm\frac{1}{2}\), and doubling the number of states. In hydrogen, spin does not change the energies (except for the tiny spin–orbit effects that we will discuss in Sec. 9.4), but it changes the counting: this is why the first shell of the periodic table holds two elements, and the second one eight.
In atoms with many electrons, the same reasoning applies to the whole atom. The atom as a whole is still rotationally symmetric, so the total orbital angular momentum, \(L\), and the total spin, \(S\), become the good quantum numbers that label its states. These are the labels of the term symbols that we will meet in Sec. 9.4.
To summarize, every quantum number we use in chemistry can be traced back to a symmetry of the system, as collected in Table 7.1.

title: 7  Spin
text:
7.5 Chapter Review

7.5.1 Key Ideas

The Stern–Gerlach experiment shows that electrons have an intrinsic angular momentum, spin, with only two possible \(z\) components, \(\pm\hbar/2\).
The spin components do not commute with each other, so measuring one of them randomizes the others.
A spin state \(c_1\alpha+c_2\beta\) gives spin up with probability \(|c_1|^2\) and spin down with probability \(|c_2|^2\).
Every quantum number comes from a symmetry of the system, through an operator that commutes with the Hamiltonian.
Spin adds a fourth label, \(m_s\), and doubles the number of states of each orbital.



7.5.2 Study Questions
1. In the Stern–Gerlach experiment, a beam of silver atoms passing through an inhomogeneous magnetic field:

is deflected into a continuous band
is not deflected
splits into three beams
is absorbed by the magnet
splits into two beams


2. The possible results of a measurement of the \(z\) component of the spin of an electron are:

\(+\hbar\) and \(-\hbar\)
\(+\frac{\hbar}{2}\) and \(-\frac{\hbar}{2}\)
\(0\) and \(\hbar\)
any value between \(-\frac{\hbar}{2}\) and \(+\frac{\hbar}{2}\)
\(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar\)


3. The magnitude of the spin of an electron, \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar\), is larger than its largest \(z\) component, \(\frac{\hbar}{2}\). This means that:

the spin always points along \(z\)
the measurement of \(S_z\) is wrong
the spin can never point exactly along the \(z\) axis
the electron has two spins
the spin is not quantized


4. An electron is described by the spin function \(c_1\alpha+c_2\beta\). The probability of measuring spin up along \(z\) is:

\(c_1\)
\(|c_2|^2\)
\(\frac{1}{2}\), whatever the coefficients
\(|c_1|^2\)
\(|c_1|^2+|c_2|^2\)


5. Electrons selected with spin up along \(z\) pass through an apparatus aligned along \(x\), and then the spin-up-along-\(x\) beam is measured again along \(z\). The result is:

both spin up and spin down along \(z\), with equal probability
only spin up along \(z\)
only spin down along \(z\)
no electrons
a continuous distribution of values


6. The commutator \([\hat{S}_x,\hat{S}_y]=i\hbar\hat{S}_z\neq0\) means that:

\(S_x\) and \(S_y\) are always zero
spin is a classical vector
the three spin components have the same value
an electron cannot have definite values of two different spin components at the same time
\(S_z\) cannot be measured


7. A quantum number is called a good quantum number when:

it is an eigenvalue of an operator that commutes with the Hamiltonian, so it does not change in time
it is an integer
it determines the energy
it is positive
it can only take two values


8. For a particle in a box placed symmetrically around \(x=0\), the energy eigenfunctions are:

all even
alternately even and odd under the reflection \(x\rightarrow-x\)
all odd
neither even nor odd
eigenfunctions of momentum


9. Why are the energy levels of a particle on a sphere \((2\ell+1)\) times degenerate?

because the Hamiltonian does not commute with \(\hat{L}_z\)
because of the Pauli exclusion principle
because the sphere has no preferred direction, so the energy cannot depend on \(m_\ell\)
because of spin
because the potential energy is \(1/r\)


10. Including spin, how many different states does the \(n=2\) level of the hydrogen atom have?

title: 8  Quantum Weirdness
text:
8.1 The double-slit experiment
In this chapter, we will delve deeper into the strangeness of quantum mechanics. In particular, we will explore quantum phenomena that don’t have a classical counterpart, starting from perhaps the simplest but also one of the most revealing: the double-slit experiment.
The double-slit experiment is considered by many the seminal experiment in quantum mechanics. The reason why we see it only at this advanced point is that its interpretation is not as straightforward as it might seem from a superficial analysis. The famous physicist Richard Feynman was so fond of this experiment that he used to say that all of quantum mechanics can be understood from carefully thinking through its implications.
The premises of the experiment are very simple: cut two slits in a solid material (such as a sheet of metal), send light or electrons through them, and observe what happens on a screen positioned at some distance on the other side. The results of this experiment, though, are far from straightforward.
Let’s first consider the single-slit case. If light consisted of classical particles, and these particles were sent in a straight line through a single-slit and allowed to strike a screen on the other side, we would expect to see a pattern corresponding to the size and shape of the slit. However, when this “single-slit experiment” is actually performed, the pattern on the screen is a diffraction pattern in which the light is spread out. The smaller the slit, the greater the angle of spread. This behavior is typical of waves, where diffraction explains the pattern as being the result of the interference of the waves with the slit.
If one illuminates two parallel slits, the light from the two slits again interferes. Here the interference is a more pronounced pattern with a series of alternating light and dark bands. The width of the bands is a property of the frequency of the illuminating light. The pattern observed on the screen is the result of this interference, as shown in Fig. 8.1.
The interference pattern resulting from the double-slit experiment is observed not only with light, but also with a beam of electrons, and other small particles. This is the same wave behavior of electrons that Davisson and Germer first observed in 1927, when they diffracted electrons from a nickel crystal (Chapter 2).

title: 8  Quantum Weirdness
text:
Figure 8.1: Diffraction through one slit (top) and interference through two slits (bottom). Left: schematic of the experiment. Right: intensity on the screen and the corresponding pattern of light and dark regions.





8.1.1 The individual particles experiment
The first twist in the plot is if we perform the experiment by sending individual particles (e.g., either individual photons, or individual electrons). Sending particles through a double-slit apparatus one at a time results in single particles appearing on the screen, as expected. Remarkably, however, an interference pattern emerges when these particles are allowed to build up one by one (Fig. 8.2). The resulting pattern on the screen is the same as if each individual particle had passed through both slits.






Figure 8.2: Simulated arrival of electrons, one at a time, on the screen of a double-slit experiment. Each electron arrives at a single random point, but as more electrons accumulate, the interference fringes emerge.



This variation of the double-slit experiment demonstrates the wave–particle duality: the particle is measured as a single pulse at a single position, while the wave describes the probability of absorbing the particle at a specific place on the screen.


8.1.2 “Which way” experiment
A second twist happens if we place particle detectors at the slits with the intent of showing through which slit a particle goes. The interference pattern in this case will disappear. The two situations are compared in Fig. 8.3. Notice that a single detector, placed on one of the two slits, is enough: if it does not click, we know that the particle went through the other slit. With the detector on, the pattern on the screen is simply the sum of the patterns produced by each slit separately, exactly what we would expect from classical particles.






Figure 8.3: The which-way experiment. Left: without a detector, the particles produce interference fringes. Right: with a detector (D) on one slit, which reveals which slit each particle goes through, the fringes disappear, and the pattern is the sum of the two single-slit patterns (dashed lines).



This experiment illustrates that photons (and electrons) can behave as either particles or waves, but cannot be observed as both at the same time. In the language that we will introduce in the next section, the interaction with the detector on the slit makes the wave function of the particle collapse onto one of the two slits, and the interference pattern is therefore lost. This result also proves that in order to measure (detect) a photon, we must interact with it, an act that changes its wave function.
The interpretation of the results of this experiment is not simple. The problem is not that we cannot describe the experiment with mathematics: the wave function predicts the interference pattern perfectly. The problem is that the wave function only gives probabilities, while each detector click, like every measurement in the macroscopic world, gives one definite result. How does a single, definite result come out of a wave function that describes all the possibilities at once? And why does looking at the slits change the outcome? These questions take us to the heart of what is called the measurement problem, the subject of the next section.

title: 8  Quantum Weirdness
section: 8.2 The Measurement Problem and Interpretations of Quantum Mechanics
text:
8.2 The Measurement Problem and Interpretations of Quantum Mechanics

8.2.1 Measurement and the collapse of the wave function
The which-way experiment shows that observing a quantum system is not a passive act: finding out which slit the particle goes through destroys the interference. To understand why, we need to look more closely at what quantum mechanics says about measurements.
In Chapter 6, we saw that if a system is in a superposition of eigenfunctions of an operator \(\hat{A}\):
\[
\Psi = \sum_i c_i \Psi_i, \qquad \hat{A}\Psi_i = a_i\Psi_i,
\tag{8.1}\]
then a measurement of the observable \(A\) can only give one of the eigenvalues \(a_i\), with probability \(|c_i|^2\). Before the measurement, we cannot predict which one we will obtain: quantum mechanics only gives us the probabilities. This raises an obvious question: what happens to the wave function after the measurement?
The answer of quantum mechanics is that, immediately after a measurement that gives the value \(a_i\), the wave function is no longer the superposition of Eq. 8.1, but the corresponding eigenfunction:
\[
\Psi \xrightarrow{\text{measurement gives } a_i} \Psi_i.
\tag{8.2}\]
This sudden change is called the collapse of the wave function. One way of seeing that it must happen is to repeat the measurement immediately after the first one: experiments show that we always obtain the same value again, \(a_i\), with certainty. This is only possible if the system is now in the eigenstate \(\Psi_i\), whose coefficient is one.
We have already seen the collapse at work in the sequential Stern–Gerlach experiments of Chapter 7 (Fig. 7.3). After the first apparatus along \(z\), the atoms in the upper beam are in the state \(\alpha\), and a second measurement along \(z\) gives “spin up” with certainty. A measurement along \(x\), however, makes the state collapse into one of the eigenstates of \(\hat{S}_x\), which are superpositions of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). When we measure along \(z\) again, we find both “spin up” and “spin down” with equal probability: the information about the first measurement has been erased by the second one. The measurement is not a “filter” that reveals a pre-existing property of the atom, but an act that changes its wave function.
The collapse is very different from the time evolution described by the TDSEq (Sec. 6.4). Time evolution is smooth, deterministic (if we know the wave function now, we can calculate it at any later time), and reversible. The collapse is sudden, random (we can only predict probabilities), and irreversible (after the collapse, we cannot reconstruct the superposition that we had before). Quantum mechanics, in its standard form, does not explain what exactly counts as a measurement, nor how or when the collapse happens. It only tells us that, when an interaction with a macroscopic instrument produces a definite result, the wave function must be updated accordingly. This is known as the measurement problem, and it is still debated by physicists and philosophers today. As we will see in this chapter, the collapse is at the heart of many of the most counterintuitive results of quantum mechanics.


8.2.2 Schrödinger’s cat and decoherence
In 1935, Erwin Schrödinger proposed a thought experiment to show how strange the measurement problem becomes when we take it seriously. A cat is sealed in a box together with a single radioactive atom, a detector, and a vial of poison. If the atom decays, the detector triggers the release of the poison, and the cat dies. After one half-life, the atom is in an equal superposition of “decayed” and “not decayed.” If the Schrödinger equation applies to everything, including the detector, the vial, and the cat, which are made of atoms too, then the cat should end up in a superposition of “alive” and “dead,” at least until someone opens the box and looks. Schrödinger did not believe in such a cat. His point was that the rules of quantum mechanics, applied blindly to a macroscopic object, lead to an absurd conclusion. Where, then, does the quantum superposition stop, and where does a definite, classical result begin?
Part of the answer comes from decoherence. A macroscopic object is never isolated: it constantly interacts with its environment, by colliding with air molecules, absorbing and emitting photons, and so on. Each of these interactions leaves a trace of the state of the object in the environment, in the same way as the detector of the which-way experiment leaves a trace of the slit that the particle went through. Once this information has spread into the environment, the different parts of the superposition can no longer interfere with each other, and the object behaves, for all practical purposes, as if it were in one state or the other, with probabilities \(|c_i|^2\). For a macroscopic object, this happens in an unimaginably short time, which is why we never see cats, or measuring devices, in superpositions. Decoherence is not an extra rule: it follows from the Schrödinger equation itself, and it has been observed in experiments, for example by watching the interference fringes of large molecules, such as fullerenes, fade away as gas is let into the interferometer. It also explains why the collapse looks irreversible: undoing it would require collecting back all the information that has been scattered into the environment.
Decoherence, however, does not solve the whole measurement problem. It explains why we never see interference between macroscopic alternatives, and why the world around us looks classical. It does not explain why each experiment has a single outcome. After decoherence, the mathematics still contains all the possibilities, the living cat and the dead cat, only now they can no longer interfere. Why we observe only one of them, and which one, is the question that decoherence leaves open. The interpretations of quantum mechanics answer it in different ways.


8.2.3 Interpretations of quantum mechanics
The mathematics of quantum mechanics is not in question: it has been tested in countless experiments, and it has never failed. What is still debated is what the mathematics means. What is the wave function: a real physical object, or just a tool to compute probabilities? Does the collapse really happen, and if so, what causes it? Do particles have definite properties before we measure them? The different answers to these questions are called interpretations of quantum mechanics.
In this textbook, as in most chemistry textbooks, we use the language of the Copenhagen interpretation, developed in the 1920s mainly by Niels Bohr and Werner Heisenberg. In this view, the wave function encodes everything that can be known about a system, it evolves according to the Schrödinger equation between measurements, and it collapses when a measurement is made, as described above. The Copenhagen interpretation is convenient for calculations, and it is the reason why we talk about “measurements” and “collapse” at all. However, it is now widely regarded as antiquated and incomplete. It divides the world into a quantum system and a classical measuring apparatus, but it never says where the boundary between the two is, nor why the apparatus, which is itself made of atoms, should not obey quantum mechanics. It adds the collapse as a separate rule, without explaining it. In other words, the Copenhagen interpretation does not solve the measurement problem; it simply declares it out of bounds.
Several modern alternatives address these shortcomings. All of them reproduce the successful predictions of quantum mechanics, but they paint very different pictures of reality:

Hidden variables. The idea that the wave function is an incomplete description, and that additional “hidden” variables determine the outcome of each measurement, goes back to Albert Einstein, who famously disliked the randomness of quantum mechanics. In 1964, John Bell proved that any theory of this kind that is also local (where nothing travels faster than light) must make predictions that differ from those of quantum mechanics. Experiments, starting in the 1970s and recognized with the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2022, have confirmed the predictions of quantum mechanics and ruled out local hidden variables. Hidden variable theories are still possible, but they must be nonlocal.
Bohmian mechanics (also called the de Broglie–Bohm or pilot-wave theory), proposed by Louis de Broglie in 1927 and developed by David Bohm in 1952, is the best known nonlocal hidden variable theory. In this view, particles always have definite positions and follow well-defined trajectories, and the wave function is a real field that guides their motion, according to an equation derived from the Schrödinger equation. There is no collapse: a measurement simply reveals where the particles already are, and the randomness of the outcomes comes from our ignorance of their exact initial positions. Bohmian mechanics is the interpretation closest to the way chemists usually think: electrons are particles that are actually somewhere, molecules have real shapes, and nuclei and electrons move along trajectories. Its price is nonlocality: the motion of each particle depends instantaneously on the positions of all the others.
Many worlds, proposed by Hugh Everett in 1957, takes the opposite route: it keeps the Schrödinger equation and nothing else. There is no collapse and no special role for measurements. When a measuring device interacts with a superposition, the device, the observer, and eventually the whole universe become part of the superposition, which splits into branches, one for each possible outcome. Each branch contains a version of the observer who sees one definite result, and decoherence prevents the branches from interacting with each other. Many worlds is the most mathematically and philosophically clean of all the interpretations, since it requires no additional rules beyond the equation that we already use. Its price is a reality much larger than the one we see, and the difficulty of explaining why the probabilities of the outcomes are given by \(|c_i|^2\) when all of them actually happen.
Spontaneous collapse theories, such as the one proposed by Giancarlo Ghirardi, Alberto Rimini, and Tullio Weber in 1986, treat the collapse as a real physical process and modify the Schrödinger equation to include it. In these theories, the wave function of any particle collapses spontaneously and at random, but extremely rarely (about once every hundred million years for a single particle). A macroscopic object, however, contains so many particles that one of them collapses almost immediately, dragging the whole object with it, which explains why we never see a cat or a measuring device in a superposition. Unlike the other interpretations, these theories make predictions that differ slightly from standard quantum mechanics, and they are currently being tested in experiments.

The main features of these interpretations are summarized in Table 8.1.



Table 8.1: Comparison of some interpretations of quantum mechanics.












Interpretation
What is the wave function?
Collapse?

Copenhagen

For the purposes of chemistry, all these interpretations give the same answers: energy levels, spectra, bond lengths, and reaction rates do not depend on which one we choose (the tiny deviations predicted by spontaneous collapse theories are far too small to affect any chemical property). This is why, in the rest of this textbook, we will keep using the convenient language of the Copenhagen interpretation. You should be aware, however, that it is a language, and not the final word on what quantum mechanics tells us about reality.

8.5 Chapter Review

8.5.1 Key Ideas

In the double-slit experiment, single particles build up an interference pattern, which disappears if we find out which slit each particle goes through.
A measurement gives one eigenvalue and collapses the wave function onto the corresponding eigenfunction.
Decoherence, the interaction with the environment, explains why we never see macroscopic superpositions such as Schrödinger’s cat, but not why each measurement gives a single result.
Different interpretations of quantum mechanics disagree on what the wave function is, but they give the same predictions for chemistry.
The uncertainty principle, \(\sigma_x\sigma_p\geq\hbar/2\), comes from the fact that the operators do not commute, not from imperfect instruments.
Particles can tunnel through barriers higher than their energy. The probability decreases exponentially with the width of the barrier and with the square root of the mass, which makes tunneling important for electrons and hydrogen atoms.

title: 9  Many-Electron Atoms
text:
9.1 Many-Electron Wave Functions
As soon as a system contains two or more electrons, the TISEq can no longer be solved analytically. Since this is the case for every atom other than hydrogen, and for every molecule other than \(\mathrm{H}_2^+\), almost all of chemistry depends on approximate methods. In this and the following chapters we will introduce the most important of these approximations, starting from many-electron atoms. Keep in mind that, precisely because they are approximations, these methods are still an active field of research, and better ones are developed every year.
The electronic Hamiltonian for an atom with \(N\) electrons can be written as:
\[
\hat{H}(\mathbf{r}_1,\mathbf{r}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{r}_N)=\sum_{i=1}^N \left(-{\frac {\hbar ^{2}}{2m_e }}\nabla_{i}^{2}-{\frac {Ze^{2}}{4\pi \varepsilon _{0}r_{i}}} \right)+{\frac {e^{2}}{4\pi \varepsilon _{0}}}\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{r_{ij}},
\tag{9.1}\]
where \(Z\) is the nuclear charge, \(m_e\) and \(e\) are respectively the mass and charge of an electron, \(\mathbf{r}_i\) and \(\nabla_i^2\) are the spatial coordinates and the Laplacian of each electron, \(r_{i}=|\mathbf{r}_i|\), and \(r_{{ij}}=|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|\) is the distance between two electrons (all other symbols have been explained in previous chapters). The TISEq is easily written using Eq. 6.22.
It is worth looking at the three pieces of this Hamiltonian one at a time:
If the third term were not there, the TISEq for the atom would separate into \(N\) hydrogen-like equations that we already know how to solve. Most of the approximations in this chapter can be understood as different ways of dealing with this single term.

9  Many-Electron Atoms

title: 9  Many-Electron Atoms
text:
9.1.1 Identical particles: fermions and bosons
When a system contains more than one electron, we need to deal with a property of quantum particles that has no classical counterpart: identical particles are truly indistinguishable. In classical mechanics, we could in principle paint one electron red and the other blue, and follow each of them along its trajectory. In quantum mechanics there are no trajectories, and two electrons are completely identical, so there is no experiment that can tell us which one is which.
To describe this mathematically, we need to include the spin of each electron. We define a variable \(\mathbf{x}\) that collects all four coordinates of an electron: the three spatial coordinates \(\mathbf{r}\), and one spin coordinate \(\mathbf{s}\), i.e., \(\mathbf{x} = \{ \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{s} \}\), and we write the wave function of \(N\) electrons as \(\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N)\). Since the electrons are indistinguishable, swapping the coordinates of any two of them cannot change any measurable quantity, and in particular it cannot change the probability density:
\[
\left|\Psi\left(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\ldots, \mathbf{x}_N\right)\right|^2=\left|\Psi\left(\mathbf{x}_2,\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots, \mathbf{x}_N\right)\right|^2.
\tag{9.2}\]
This equation can be satisfied in two ways: the wave function can stay the same when we swap two particles (it is symmetric), or it can change sign (it is antisymmetric). Nature uses both options, for two different families of particles:

Bosons have symmetric wave functions. Photons and helium-4 atoms are examples of bosons.
Fermions have antisymmetric wave functions. Electrons, protons, and neutrons are fermions.

Which family a particle belongs to is determined by its spin: particles with integer spin (\(s=0,1,2,\ldots\)) are bosons, and particles with half-integer spin (\(s=\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\ldots\)) are fermions. This connection is known as the spin-statistics theorem, and it can be proven only in the framework of relativistic quantum mechanics, so we will simply accept it here. Since electrons have \(s=\frac{1}{2}\) (Chapter 7), they are fermions, and their wave function must be antisymmetric with respect to the exchange of any two of them:
\[
\Psi\left(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\ldots, \mathbf{x}_N\right) = - \Psi\left(\mathbf{x}_2,\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots, \mathbf{x}_N\right)
\tag{9.3}\]
This simple requirement has an enormous consequence. Suppose that we try to describe two electrons with exactly the same state, including their spin, so that \(\mathbf{x}_1=\mathbf{x}_2\). Swapping two identical things cannot change anything, so the wave function must be unchanged by the swap. At the same time, Eq. 9.3 says that it must change sign. The only number that is equal to minus itself is zero, so the wave function must vanish: two electrons can never be in the same state. This is the Pauli exclusion principle, which we will see again, in a more familiar form, when we build many-electron wave functions below. Bosons, instead, have no such restriction, and any number of them can be described by the same state. This difference is responsible for the shell structure of atoms, and therefore for the whole of chemistry: if electrons were bosons, all of them would be described by the \(1s\) orbital, and atoms would not form bonds the way they do.


9.1.2 Spin-orbitals and Slater determinants
A very important step in simplifying \(\Psi(\mathbf{x})\) is to build it from one-electron functions. Since we need to take the spin coordinate into account as well, we define a new function, called spin-orbital, by multiplying a spatial orbital by one of the two spin functions, \(\alpha\) (spin up, \(m_s=+\frac{1}{2}\)) or \(\beta\) (spin down, \(m_s=-\frac{1}{2}\)), that we introduced in Chapter 7:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\chi(\mathbf{x}) &= \psi(\mathbf{r}) \alpha(\mathbf{s}), \\
\chi(\mathbf{x}) &= \psi(\mathbf{r}) \beta(\mathbf{s}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.4}\]
For a given spatial orbital \(\psi(\mathbf{r})\) we can therefore form two spin-orbitals, one with spin up and one with spin down (the spin coordinate \(\mathbf{s}\) has only two possible values, as we discussed in Chapter 7). For the spatial orbitals we can use the same one-electron functions that solve the TISEq for the hydrogen atom, \(\psi_{n\ell m_{\ell}}(\mathbf{r})\) (Eq. 5.5 in Chapter 5). Each spin-orbital then depends on four quantum numbers: the three of the spatial part, \(n,\ell,m_{\ell}\), plus the spin quantum number \(m_s\). We need to keep in mind, however, that the spin-orbitals \(\chi_{n\ell m_{\ell} m_{s}}\) are not solutions of the many-electron TISEq, so any wave function that we build from them is an approximation, not the exact wave function of the system.
Once we have spin-orbitals, we can use them as the building blocks of the many-electron wave function, making sure that the result is antisymmetric. We start from the simplest case: two electrons, with coordinates \(\mathbf{x}_1\) and \(\mathbf{x}_2\), and two spin-orbitals, \(\chi_1\) and \(\chi_2\). The most general wave function that we can build from products of these two spin-orbitals is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) =& b_{11} \chi_1(\mathbf{x}_1) \chi_1(\mathbf{x}_2) + b_{12} \chi_1(\mathbf{x}_1) \chi_2(\mathbf{x}_2) + \\
& b_{21} \chi_2(\mathbf{x}_1) \chi_1(\mathbf{x}_2) + b_{22} \chi_2(\mathbf{x}_1) \chi_2(\mathbf{x}_2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.5}\]
For this function to change sign when we swap \(\mathbf{x}_1\) and \(\mathbf{x}_2\), we need \(b_{12} = -b_{21}\) and \(b_{11} = b_{22} = 0\), which gives:
\[
\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) = b_{12} \left[ \chi_1(\mathbf{x}_1) \chi_2(\mathbf{x}_2) - \chi_2(\mathbf{x}_1) \chi_1(\mathbf{x}_2)\right].
\tag{9.6}\]
This wave function is sufficient to describe two-electron atoms and ions, such as helium. The coefficient is fixed by the normalization condition, \(b_{12} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). For the ground state of helium, we can use the \(1s\) hydrogen-like orbital, \(\psi_{100}\), as the spatial part of both spin-orbitals, obtaining:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left[ \psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_1)\alpha(1) \; \psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_2)\beta(2) - \psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_1)\beta(1) \; \psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_2)\alpha(2) \right] \\
&= \psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_1)\psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_2) \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left[ \alpha(1)\beta(2) - \beta(1)\alpha(2) \right],
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.7}\]
where \(\alpha(1)\) is short for \(\alpha(\mathbf{s}_1)\), and so on. This equation shows that we need just one spatial orbital, \(\psi_{100}\), to describe the system, while the antisymmetry is taken care of by the combination of spin functions, \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left[ \alpha(1)\beta(2) - \beta(1)\alpha(2) \right]\). Notice that we commit a small inaccuracy when we say that “two electrons occupy one spatial orbital, one electron has spin up, and the other electron has spin down,” as is typically done in general chemistry textbooks with the configuration \([\uparrow\downarrow]\). The real spin state is more subtle: neither electron individually is “the up one”; instead, the ground state of helium is the combination \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\uparrow\downarrow-\downarrow\uparrow\right]\).
To go from two electrons to \(N\), we can first observe that Eq. 9.6 is exactly the determinant of a \(2\times2\) matrix built from the spin-orbitals:
\[
\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2)= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{\left|\begin{matrix} \chi_1(\mathbf{x}_1)&\chi_2(\mathbf{x}_1)\\\chi_1(\mathbf{x}_2)&\chi_2(\mathbf{x}_2)
\end{matrix}\right|},
\tag{9.8}\]
where each column contains one spin-orbital, each row contains the coordinates of one electron, and the vertical bars mean that we take the determinant of the matrix. This construction is called a Slater determinant, and it is the standard way of building an \(N\)-electron wave function. Slater determinants can be written for any number of electrons, using the same number of spin-orbitals, and they automatically produce an antisymmetric wave function. A general Slater determinant is written:
\[
\Psi (\mathbf{x} _{1},\mathbf{x} _{2},\ldots ,\mathbf{x} _{N})={\frac {1}{\sqrt {N!}}}{\left|\begin{matrix}\chi _{1}(\mathbf{x} _{1})&\chi _{2}(\mathbf{x} _{1})&\cdots &\chi _{N}(\mathbf{x} _{1})\\\chi _{1}(\mathbf{x} _{2})&\chi _{2}(\mathbf{x} _{2})&\cdots &\chi _{N}(\mathbf{x} _{2})\\\vdots &\vdots &\ddots &\vdots \\\chi _{1}(\mathbf{x} _{N})&\chi _{2}(\mathbf{x} _{N})&\cdots &\chi _{N}(\mathbf{x} _{N})\end{matrix}\right|} = |\chi _{1}\,\chi _{2}\cdots \chi _{N}|,
\tag{9.9}\]
where the notation \(|\cdots|\) on the right is a compact shorthand for the whole determinant (including its normalization factor), in which we only list the spin-orbitals that appear on its diagonal. When a spin-orbital is used in the Slater determinant to describe an electron, we say that it is occupied, and orbitals that are not used are called unoccupied (or virtual). This is convenient language, and we will use it throughout the textbook, but it should not be taken literally: orbitals are not boxes that contain electrons, but mathematical functions that we use to describe them.
Two properties of determinants that you may remember from linear algebra have important physical consequences here:

Swapping two rows changes the sign of a determinant. Swapping two rows means swapping the coordinates of two electrons, so a Slater determinant is always antisymmetric, as required by Eq. 9.3.
A determinant with two identical columns is zero. If we try to describe two electrons with the same spin-orbital (same \(n,\ell,m_\ell\), and same \(m_s\)), two columns become identical and the wave function vanishes everywhere. In other words, such a state does not exist. This is the familiar form of the Pauli exclusion principle from general chemistry, “no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers,” which here appears as a direct consequence of the antisymmetry of the wave function.

9.2 Approximated Hamiltonians
To solve the TISEq for a many-electron atom we also need to deal with the Hamiltonian, since analytic solutions of the full Hamiltonian in Eq. 9.1 cannot be found. The most important tool that chemists use for this purpose is called the variational method.

9.2.1 Variational method
The idea behind the variational method is simple. We guess a “trial” wave function that contains some adjustable numbers, called variational parameters. We then calculate the energy of the trial function and change the parameters until this energy is as low as possible. The trial function with the lowest energy, and that energy itself, are our best approximations to the true ground-state wave function and energy.
Why should the lowest energy be the best answer? The energy of a trial function \(\Phi\) is the expectation value of the Hamiltonian:
\[
E[\Phi] = \frac{\int \Phi^* {\hat H} \Phi d\mathbf{\tau}}{\int \Phi^* \Phi d\mathbf{\tau}},
\tag{9.10}\]
where \(\mathbf{\tau}=\left(\mathbf{r}_1,\mathbf{r}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{r}_N\right)\) collects the spatial coordinates of all electrons, so the integrals are \(3N\)-dimensional. The denominator takes care of normalization, so \(\Phi\) does not need to be normalized. The justification of the method is the variational theorem: the energy calculated from any trial wave function is always greater than or equal to the exact ground-state energy, \(\mathcal{E}_0\):
\[
E[\Phi] \geq \mathcal{E}_0.
\tag{9.11}\]
and the equality holds only if \(\Phi\) is the exact ground state. In other words, we can never “overshoot” the exact energy from below. This gives us a clear strategy: any change in the trial function that lowers its energy brings the energy closer to the exact answer. (As the energy goes down, the wave function usually gets better too, although “better” for a wave function is harder to define than for a number, and it is guaranteed to be exact only when \(\Phi = \Psi_0\).)






NoteProof: the variational theorem





The proof uses a nice trick. Even if we cannot solve the TISEq, its exact eigenfunctions \(\Psi_i\) (with energies \(\mathcal{E}_0 \leq \mathcal{E}_1 \leq \mathcal{E}_2 \leq \ldots\)) still exist and form a complete set. We can therefore imagine expanding our trial function in terms of them:
\[
\Phi = \sum_i c_i \Psi_i.
\tag{9.12}\]
We never need to know the \(\Psi_i\) or the \(c_i\); the expansion is only a tool for the proof. Inserting it in Eq. 9.10, we obtain:
\[
E[\Phi] = \frac{\sum_{ij} c_i^* c_j \int \Psi_i^* {\hat H} \Psi_jd\mathbf{\tau}}{
\sum_{ij} c_i^* c_j \int \Psi_i^* \Psi_jd\mathbf{\tau}}.
\tag{9.13}\]
Since each \(\Psi_j\) is an eigenfunction of \({\hat H}\), we can replace \({\hat H} \Psi_j\) with \(\mathcal{E}_j \Psi_j\):
\[
E[\Phi] = \frac{\sum_{ij} c_i^* c_j \mathcal{E}_j \int \Psi_i^* \Psi_j d\mathbf{\tau}}{
\sum_{ij} c_i^* c_j \int \Psi_i^* \Psi_j d\mathbf{\tau}}.
\tag{9.14}\]
The eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator are orthonormal (or can be chosen to be, Chapter 6), so all integrals with \(i\neq j\) vanish and those with \(i=j\) are equal to one:
\[
E[\Phi] = \frac{\sum_{i} |c_i|^2 \mathcal{E}_i}{\sum_{i} |c_i|^2}.
\tag{9.15}\]
This equation already tells the whole story: the energy of the trial function is a weighted average of the exact energies, with weights \(|c_i|^2\), and an average can never be lower than its smallest member. To make this explicit, we subtract \(\mathcal{E}_0\) from both sides:
\[
E[\Phi] - \mathcal{E}_0 = \frac{\sum_i |c_i|^2 ( \mathcal{E}_i - \mathcal{E}_0)}{
\sum_i |c_i|^2}.
\tag{9.16}\]
Every term on the right-hand side is greater than or equal to zero, because \(|c_i|^2\geq0\) and \(\mathcal{E}_i \geq \mathcal{E}_0\). Therefore, \(E[\Phi] \geq \mathcal{E}_0\).





9.2.2 Approximated solution for the helium atom
We now have all the ingredients for the simplest approximate solution of the TISEq for a many-electron atom. We start by writing the wave function as the Slater determinant of Eq. 9.9, in which each spatial orbital is used to describe two electrons of opposite spin:
\[
\Psi (\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots ,\mathbf{x}_{N})= |\chi_{1}\,\chi_{2}\cdots \chi_{N}| = |\psi_{1}\alpha\;\psi_{1}\beta\cdots \psi_{\frac{N}{2}}\alpha\;\psi_{\frac{N}{2}}\beta|,
\tag{9.17}\]
and we insert it into the TISEq for \(N\) electrons. This results in a set of \(N\) one-electron equations, one for each electron. When we try to solve each of them, however, we run into the problem that we identified at the beginning of this chapter: because of the electron-electron repulsion term, the potential felt by each electron does not have spherical symmetry, and the one-electron TISEq cannot be solved in spherical polar coordinates as we did for the hydrogen atom in Chapter 5. The crudest way around the problem is to neglect the electron-electron repulsion altogether (i.e., to pretend that the electrons do not interact with each other). For a two-electron atom the Hamiltonian then becomes a sum of two one-electron Hamiltonians:
\[
\hat{H} =\hat{H}_1+\hat{H}_2,
\tag{9.18}\]
each of them identical to the Hamiltonian of a hydrogen-like atom with nuclear charge \(Z\). This Hamiltonian does not depend on spin, so we can drop the spin part of Eq. 9.7 and write the wave function for the ground state of helium simply as:
\[
\Psi(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2) = \psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_1)\psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_2).
\tag{9.19}\]
The TISEq then separates into two independent one-electron equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{H}_1 \psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_1) &= E_1\psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_1) \\
\hat{H}_2 \psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_2) &= E_2\psi_{100}(\mathbf{r}_2),
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.20}\]
which we already know how to solve (Chapter 5), and whose solutions combine to give:
\[
E = E_1+E_2.
\tag{9.21}\]
In this approximation, the energy of the helium atom is twice the energy of a \(1s\) electron in a hydrogen-like atom with \(Z=2\). The energies in Eq. 5.7 scale as \(Z^2\) when the nuclear charge is \(Z\) instead of \(1\), so the \(1s\) energy is \(-\frac{Z^2}{2}E_h\) and the total is \(E=2\times\left(-\frac{Z^2}{2}\right)E_h=-4\,E_h\), or about \(-10{,}500 \text{ kJ/mol}\),1 compared with the exact value of \(-2.9037\,E_h=-7{,}624 \text{ kJ/mol}\). The error is enormous, about \(40\%\), because we have neglected a large positive contribution to the energy. We can partially fix it by keeping the same orbitals and adding back the average repulsion between the two electrons, which for two \(1s\) electrons is \(\frac{5}{8}Z\,E_h\) (\(1.25\,E_h=3{,}282\text{ kJ/mol}\) for helium). The result, \(-2.75\,E_h = -7{,}220 \text{ kJ/mol}\), is already much better, with an error of about \(5\%\).

Optimizing the effective nuclear charge
We can do better using the variational method. The two electrons do not feel the full charge of the nucleus, since each of them is partially shielded from it by the other. We can account for this by using, for both electrons, a \(1s\) orbital with an adjustable charge \(\zeta\) in place of \(Z\):
\[
\psi_{1s}(r) = \sqrt{\frac{\zeta^3}{\pi a_0^3}}\, e^{-\zeta r/a_0},
\tag{9.22}\]
and treat \(\zeta\) as a variational parameter. Calculating the expectation value of the full Hamiltonian, Eq. 9.1, with \(\Psi=\psi_{1s}(\mathbf{r}_1)\psi_{1s}(\mathbf{r}_2)\), gives three contributions (in \(E_h\)): the kinetic energy of the two electrons, \(\zeta^2\); their attraction to the nucleus of charge \(Z\), \(-2Z\zeta\); and their mutual repulsion, \(+\frac{5}{8}\zeta\). Summing them:
\[
E(\zeta) = \zeta^2 - 2Z\zeta + \frac{5}{8}\zeta.
\tag{9.23}\]
This energy is plotted in Fig. 9.1. To find its minimum, we set the derivative to zero:
\[
\frac{dE}{d\zeta} = 2\zeta - 2Z + \frac{5}{8} = 0 \quad\longrightarrow\quad \zeta_{\text{min}} = Z - \frac{5}{16} = 1.6875,
\tag{9.24}\]
and replacing this value in Eq. 9.23 gives \(E(\zeta_{\text{min}}) = -\left(Z-\frac{5}{16}\right)^2 = -2.8477\,E_h = -7{,}477 \text{ kJ/mol}\).






Figure 9.1: Variational energy of the helium atom as a function of the orbital exponent \(\zeta\). The orange dot is the energy of the unshielded orbitals (\(\zeta=Z=2\), with the average repulsion included), the purple dot is the variational minimum, and the dotted line is the exact energy.



Let’s see what these results tell us:

The variational theorem at work: every point of the curve in Fig. 9.1 lies above the exact energy, as guaranteed by Eq. 9.11. The minimum gets within \(147 \text{ kJ/mol}\) (about \(2\%\)) of the exact value, using a single adjustable number.
Shielding: the optimal value \(\zeta_{\text{min}}=1.6875\) is smaller than the real nuclear charge, \(Z=2\). We can interpret it as the effective nuclear charge, \(Z_\text{eff}\), felt by each electron. Each electron spends part of its time between the nucleus and the other electron, partially canceling the attraction that the other electron feels. The amount of shielding, \(\frac{5}{16}\approx0.31\) of a proton charge, is much less than a full electron charge because the two electrons occupy the same region of space: a \(1s\) electron is only rarely found “inside” the other one.
Orbital size: since \(\langle r\rangle \propto 1/\zeta\), a smaller effective charge means a larger orbital. The shielded \(1s\) orbitals of helium are about \(2/1.6875\approx1.19\) times larger than the unshielded ones.
What is still missing: even the best possible orbitals cannot reach the exact energy if we keep the product form of Eq. 9.19. We will come back to this point at the end of this chapter, when we discuss electron correlation.

The results obtained with the different approximations are summarized in Fig. 9.2, which also reports the Hartree–Fock limit that we will discuss in the next chapter.






Figure 9.2: Energy of the helium atom computed with the approximations discussed in this chapter, compared with the exact value.

9.3 Shielding and Penetration
The helium example shows that the main effect of the other electrons on any given electron is to reduce the nuclear charge that it feels. We can generalize this idea to any atom by writing the effective nuclear charge felt by an electron as:
\[
Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - \sigma,
\tag{9.25}\]
where \(\sigma\) is called the shielding constant, and it measures how much the other electrons screen the nucleus. In the simplest model of a many-electron atom, called the central-field approximation, each electron moves in the field of the nucleus plus the spherically averaged field of all other electrons. Since this effective potential depends only on \(r\), the angular part of the TISEq is the same as for hydrogen, and the orbitals keep the familiar shapes of the spherical harmonics and the labels \(n\), \(\ell\), \(m_\ell\). The radial part, however, changes, and with it the energies. What the central-field approximation does not include is the instantaneous repulsion between electrons: each electron feels only the average position of the others, not where they actually are at any given moment.
Inner-shell electrons are very effective at shielding the outer ones, while electrons of the same shell shield each other only partially (as we saw for helium). As a result, outer electrons feel a much smaller effective charge than inner electrons, they are held less tightly, and their orbitals are more diffuse. This explains why the valence electrons of an atom are the ones involved in chemistry, while the core electrons are not.
The most important consequence of shielding, however, is that it breaks the degeneracy of orbitals with the same \(n\) and different \(\ell\). Recall from Chapter 5 that in the hydrogen atom the \(2s\) and \(2p\) orbitals have exactly the same energy. In a many-electron atom this is no longer the case. To understand why, consider the lithium atom, which has two core electrons, described by the \(1s\) orbital, and one valence electron. The radial probability distributions of the \(2s\) and \(2p\) orbitals, compared with that of the \(1s^2\) core, are plotted in Fig. 9.3.






Figure 9.3: Radial probability distributions of the \(2s\) and \(2p\) orbitals of lithium compared with the \(1s^2\) core (gray), computed using hydrogen-like functions with effective nuclear charges. The radial node of the \(2s\) orbital is highlighted with a purple dot.



The \(2s\) orbital has a small inner lobe, the one that we already noticed for hydrogen in Chapter 5, which places part of its probability inside the \(1s^2\) core. When it is there, a \(2s\) electron feels almost the full nuclear charge. We say that the \(2s\) orbital penetrates the core. The \(2p\) orbital, instead, starts at zero at the nucleus and has no inner lobe, so it is more effectively shielded by the core electrons. As a result, a \(2s\) electron feels a larger \(Z_\text{eff}\) than a \(2p\) electron, and it is lower in energy. This is the \(2s\)–\(2p\) splitting that general chemistry textbooks show in their orbital energy diagrams. In general, for the same \(n\), penetration decreases as \(\ell\) increases (because of the \(r^\ell\) behavior of the radial functions close to the nucleus), so the energies of the orbitals follow the order \(ns < np < nd < nf\).
The effective nuclear charges felt by the \(1s\), \(2s\), and \(2p\) electrons of the second-row atoms can be obtained from variational calculations similar to the one we did for helium. Some of the results are reported in Table 9.1.

Notice how the \(1s\) electrons feel almost the full nuclear charge (they are shielded only by each other, as in helium), while the valence electrons feel a much smaller charge. Notice also how \(Z_\text{eff}(2s)\) is larger than \(Z_\text{eff}(2p)\), as expected from penetration, although the difference becomes small for the heavier atoms of the row. When the electrons of an atom are described using the orbitals in order of increasing energy, following the Pauli exclusion principle, the different penetration of \(s\), \(p\), \(d\), and \(f\) orbitals produces the familiar aufbau order, \(1s<2s<2p<3s<3p<4s<3d<\ldots\), and with it the structure of the periodic table.
